data.title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Spending Contracts For Latest AI-Driven Startup Batch
data.ai_summary: Ten U.S. startups raised over $1.5 billion in funding this week, with Modal Labs leading at $750 million and Icon at $200 million. Other rounds included biotech, insurance, and AI sectors, with most deals in the $60-135 million range.

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

Startup investors aren’t exactly hitting pause, but they did scale back on giant rounds this past week, with just two startup financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. The biggest round went to AI infrastructure provider Modal Labs, which picked up $750 million, followed by construction automation unicorn Icon, which secured $200 million. Other sectors that attracted larger rounds this past week included biotech, insurance and AI.

1. Modal Labs, $750M, AI infrastructure: Modal Labs, a provider of cloud infrastructure for AI inference and other applications, secured $750 million in a Series D funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation. The New York-headquartered company said it recently exceeded an annual revenue run rate of $1 billion.

2. Icon, $200M, construction tech: Austin-based Icon, a developer of robotic construction systems known for its 3D-printed homes, closed on $200 million in Series D funding led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock. The company says it is on pace for 4x revenue growth in 2026.

3. Soufflé Therapeutics, $135M, RNA therapies: Boston-based Soufflé Therapeutics, a developer of RNA therapies, raised $135 million in Series B funding led by Juvia Group as part of a large syndicate of investors.

4. Estuary Biotherapeutics, $103M, gene therapies: Menlo Park, California-based Estuary Biotherapeutics, a developer of genetic medicines for patients with serious kidney diseases, launched with $103 million in financing. The funding includes $93 million in a Series A round led by RA Capital Management as well as $10 million in previously undisclosed seed capital.

5. Labelbox, $100M, AI tools: Labelbox, a developer of technology to train and evaluate AI models and to help deploy agents that improve with experience, picked up $100 million in Series E funding. Infinitum Partners led the financing for the 8-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

6. Suki, $90M, health AI: Redwood City, California-based Suki, a provider of AI tools that turn clinical conversations into intelligence for documentation, coding and other healthcare workflows, announced a $90 million Series E financing from backers including Healthier Capital and Crosslink Capital.

7. Abby Care, $82M, caregiver platform: Abby Care, a platform for family members to become certified, paid caregivers and deliver care at home, closed on $82 million in Series C funding, per a Fortune report. Transformation Capital led the financing for the 5-year-old, San Francisco-based startup.

8. Stand, $70M, insurance: Stand, a provider of insurance for homes in areas at higher risk of natural disasters, secured $70 million in Series C funding at a $1 billion valuation. Saga Ventures led the financing for the 3-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

9. Mueon, $65M, semiconductor systems: Mueon Corp., a semiconductor systems company building a modular platform for AI and hyperscale computing, completed a $65 million Series A funding round. Maverick Silicon led the financing for the Portland, Oregon-based company.

10. North.cloud, $60M, AI spend management: New York-based North.cloud, provider of an infrastructure spend intelligence and automation platform, raised $60 million in a Series B round led by PeakSpan Capital.

Methodology

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 10-16, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

data.title: Labelbox Raises Over $100M to Expand AI Training and Enterprise Agents
data.ai_summary: Labelbox raised over $100 million in Series E financing led by Infinitum Partners. The company will use the funds to expand its reinforcement learning infrastructure and enterprise AI agent business, serving over 400 customers including most leading U.S. AI labs.
data.author: Win Warfield
data.full_text:
San Francisco-based Labelbox has raised more than $100 million in Series E financing led by Infinitum Partners, with participation from Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, Snowpoint Ventures, and other investors. The company seeks to expand its reinforcement learning infrastructure and enterprise AI agent business, as developers seek ways to improve models beyond their initial training.
Labelbox has developed two principal products. One called Horizon provides reinforcement learning environments and evaluation infrastructure for AI labs, letting models practice multistep tasks, receive feedback, and improve performance. The second, Recursion Managed Agents, targets enterprise customers. The company’s platform allows businesses to deploy groups of AI agents within existing applications, initiating tasks in response to schedules, alerts, and tickets.
“Every company will soon run on AI systems that learn from their own work. Getting there takes innovation at every layer, from sandbox infrastructure and the agent harness to reinforcement learning post-training. Labelbox brings those layers together in one platform, and this funding lets us push each one further, so that frontier labs and enterprises can build AI that gets better with every run,” said Manu Sharma, co-founder and CEO of Labelbox.
Sharma’s career has spanned aerospace engineering, robotics and software platforms. Before co-founding Labelbox, Sharma worked as a product manager at Planet Labs from 2017 to 2018, helping develop software for analyzing satellite imagery. As an early engineer at DroneDeploy, from 2014 to 2017, he worked on drone flight-control systems and the company’s application marketplace.
Earlier, Sharma co-founded Ardulab, also known as Infinity Aerospace, at NASA Ames Research Park. The venture developed open-source laboratory platforms for conducting scientific experiments aboard the International Space Station.
Labelbox said it serves more than 400 customers, including over 90% of leading U.S. AI labs. The company also uses more than 50 agents internally across engineering, research, product, sales, marketing and finance. It opened Recursion Managed Agents to enterprise customers earlier in October, extending a platform it previously used internally.
As AI developers seek to improve model reliability and close the gap between benchmark performance and real-world execution, Labelbox’s strategy combines training infrastructure with managed agents, potentially linking model development to enterprise deployment.

Labelbox raised more than $100 million in Series E financing at a $1.25 billion pre money valuation. The round combines equity with a credit facility and was led by Infinitum Partners, with participation from Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, Snowpoint Ventures, and others. The capital will accelerate research and engineering on the company’s two core products, Horizon (reinforcement learning environments and evaluation tools for frontier AI labs) and Recursion Managed Agents (enterprise agents that operate inside existing business applications and improve with every run), along with expansion of the teams that deliver them to customers. Access to compute is positioned as central to the next phase; Infinitum’s John Yetimoglu, an early Groq investor now involved in large scale compute infrastructure at GroqCloud, brings relevant experience. Labelbox, founded in 2018 in San Francisco by Manu Sharma (CEO), Brian Rieger, and Dan Rasmuson, has progressed through three distinct chapters: Data chapter : Tools for capturing expert judgment and converting it into high quality training data. Many large technology companies still use the platform for enterprise post training programs.

: After the rise of transformers and RLHF, Labelbox built Horizon so frontier models could practice real work rather than learn only from static examples. The company now works with more than 90% of leading U.S. AI labs and hyperscalers. Agents chapter: Models can perform real work, but traditional assistants still require constant human direction. Labelbox first built autonomous agents for its own operations (more than 50 agents now run across engineering, research, product, sales, marketing, and finance) then opened the system to external customers as Recursion Managed Agents in early October 2026. The company reports more than 400 customers spanning frontier labs, hyperscalers, startups, and Fortune 500 firms. It reached profitability in 2026 while growing more than fivefold year over year. Horizon: Reinforcement Learning Infrastructure for Frontier Labs Horizon supplies RL environments, expert feedback, and evaluation infrastructure for post training frontier models. Its WorldSim component constructs realistic simulated companies filled with code, dashboards, spreadsheets, decks, and documents. Models attempt multi step tasks end to end; every step is recorded as a trajectory. Deterministic verifiers score correctness consistently, while expert preference signals teach “taste” when multiple trajectories succeed. The platform operates at the scale of thousands of worlds and millions of graded trajectories, covering coding, computer use, research, multimodal, and voice domains, tuned to labs’ pass@k targets. Recursion Managed Agents: Enterprise Agents That Improve Themselves Recursion Managed Agents receive a goal, a trigger (schedule, alert, Slack message, webhook, or API call), and a rubric defining quality. A separate grader scores every run against the rubric and supplies evidence; agents revise when they fall short. Agents operate in multi agent (coordinator + specialists), team (parallel copies on a shared board), or auto modes. They connect to more than 100 business applications and any MCP server, with tools scoped by permission level and credentials held in a vault. Sessions run in isolated sandboxes with zero data retention at LLM providers. Compliance includes SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, CCPA, NIST 800-171, and PCI DSS. Pricing is per agent session hour. Internally, Labelbox runs 51 agents across 11 teams. In one documented example, a pull request review agent reduced median cost 32% across successive graded reviews while maintaining quality, with memory updated multiple times. Memory is curated automatically (once five new session reports exist, and at most once per hour) and remains reviewable and editable by customers. Both Horizon and Recursion rest on the same underlying principle: systems that improve from their own work through reflection on prior sessions, curated memory, and the ability to fine tune on their best outputs. Labelbox owns the full stack, agent harness for long horizon work, sandbox infrastructure running millions of VMs, its own RL post training systems, and an expert network of more than 4 million people, allowing the layers to be co-designed and optimized together. Series A (2019): $10 million

Series B (2020): $25 million (led by a16z)

Series D (January 2022): $110 million (led by SoftBank Vision Fund II, valuation near or at $950 million–$1 billion range) The Series E marks the first major equity raise in more than four and a half years and lifts the pre money valuation to $1.25 billion. The inclusion of a credit facility alongside equity is consistent with a profitable, rapidly growing company seeking to fund infrastructure and compute without excessive dilution. The raise underscores a broader industry shift from pure model scale toward systems that learn continuously from real work and experience. Labelbox sits at the intersection of RL post training infrastructure (serving the frontier labs that set the capability frontier) and production agent platforms (serving enterprises that must operationalize those capabilities inside existing tools and workflows). Profitability combined with 5x+ growth provides a strong foundation; the new capital and compute relationships position the company to expand both product depth and go to market reach simultaneously. Labelbox’s internal use of its own agents as a live proving ground, its ownership of the full technology stack, and its deep penetration among leading AI labs give it a distinctive position as the field moves from static training data and one shot assistants toward recursive, self improving AI systems. data.title: Labelbox Raises Over $100 Million in Series E Funding
data.ai_summary: Labelbox raised over $100 million in Series E financing led by Infinitum Partners, with participation from Wipro Ventures, a16z, and others. The company reached profitability in 2026 and grew more than fivefold year over year. The funding will support research and engineering for its Horizon and Recursion Managed Agents products.
data.full_text:
Labelbox, an AI platform supporting reinforcement learning for frontier models and managed agents for enterprises, has announced more than US$100 million in Series E financing. The round includes both equity and a credit facility and was led by Infinitum Partners, with participation from Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, Snowpoint Ventures, and others. The company disclosed the funding alongside news that it reached profitability in 2026 while growing more than fivefold year over year.
Funding and Growth
Labelbox works with more than 400 customers, including over 90% of leading U.S. AI labs, hyperscalers, startups, and Fortune 500 companies. The Series E financing will support continued research and engineering across Horizon and Recursion Managed Agents, as well as expansion of the teams bringing these products to customers. The company also plans to deepen its work with leading AI labs and hyperscalers on post-training programs.
Platform Approach
As AI models become capable of performing increasingly complex tasks, the next challenge is enabling them to learn from experience and reliably execute work in real-world environments. Labelbox is addressing this opportunity through two core products, Horizon and Recursion Managed Agents. Horizon focuses on reinforcement learning and evaluation for frontier labs, while Recursion Managed Agents supports enterprise fleets of agents that improve with every run.
Horizon for Frontier Labs
Horizon provides reinforcement learning environments, expert feedback, and evaluation infrastructure that help AI labs train and improve frontier models. Its environments simulate complex, multi-step work across coding, research, and other demanding tasks, enabling models to practice, receive feedback on their performance, and improve through reinforcement learning. Labelbox works with leading AI labs and hyperscalers on post-training programs that rely on these structured practice environments.
Recursion Managed Agents
Recursion Managed Agents enables companies to deploy fleets of AI agents inside the applications their teams already use. Agents can initiate work in response to schedules, alerts, tickets, and other triggers, coordinate across tools, and have their output evaluated against defined standards. Each completed run can inform the agent's memory, helping it improve how it approaches future tasks without manual retraining.
Leadership Perspective
"Every company will soon run on AI systems that learn from their own work," said Manu Sharma, CEO and co-founder of Labelbox. He noted that getting there takes innovation at every layer, from sandbox infrastructure and the agent harness to reinforcement learning post-training. Sharma added that Labelbox brings those layers together in one platform, and this funding lets the company push each one further so that frontier labs and enterprises can build AI that gets better with every run.
Enterprise Adoption
Labelbox already uses more than 50 agents internally across functions including engineering, research, product, sales, marketing, and finance. Earlier this month, the company opened Recursion Managed Agents to enterprise customers, extending its approach to continuous improvement beyond AI research labs. The platform lets enterprises deploy fleets of agents that coordinate across tools, respond to triggers such as schedules and tickets, and improve with every run.
With this Series E funding, Labelbox aims to help both frontier labs and enterprises build AI systems that learn from their own work and improve over time. The company combines agent infrastructure, sandbox environments, and reinforcement learning post-training systems to support the development and deployment of AI systems across demanding real-world tasks. Its profitability, fivefold year-over-year growth, and expanding customer base signal rising demand for AI platforms that enable continuous learning and reliable execution.

data.title: Startup Funding News Today, October 15, 2026: Modal, Labelbox, OMass Therapeutics, Skeleton Technologies & More
data.ai_summary: Over $1.51 billion in funding flowed into 10 startups over 24 hours, led by Modal's $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation. OMass Therapeutics raised $310 million for hormonal and autoimmune treatments, while Skeleton Technologies secured over $100 million in Siemens-led financing. The activity reflects investor focus on AI infrastructure and specialized technologies.
data.author: Nickie Louise
data.full_text:
0 Shares

More than $1.51 billion in newly announced funding transactions flowed into 10 major startups over the past 24 hours, alongside a separate €50 million investment in France. The biggest deals reveal a venture market financing two very different priorities: the infrastructure needed to run artificial intelligence at scale and specialized technologies that can solve expensive problems in healthcare, manufacturing, energy, and enterprise operations. San Francisco-based Modal led the day’s funding activity with a $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation, after reporting that its annualized revenue run rate surpassed $1 billion. Oxford biotech startup OMass Therapeutics secured $310 million to advance experimental treatments for hormonal and autoimmune diseases. Meanwhile, European energy-storage company Skeleton Technologies raised more than $100 million in Siemens-led financing, becoming a unicorn as it expands into the U.S. AI data center market. The activity extends across several layers of the AI economy. Salience Labs raised $125 million to commercialize optical networking chips that connect increasingly large GPU clusters. Labelbox announced more than $100 million in financing for reinforcement learning and enterprise AI agents. Harmonic Security secured $50 million to address the security risks created by employee AI use, while Duvo raised $32 million to automate operational processes across retailers and consumer-goods companies. Beyond AI software, India’s Scimplify raised $25 million to expand specialty-chemical and critical-materials production, with Hitachi Ventures leading the investment. France’s Dougs secured €50 million to accelerate AI-based accounting services. Boston-based Tamr raised $21 million to improve the fragmented enterprise data that increasingly autonomous AI systems depend on. The broader signal is that investors are financing the systems that make AI commercially useful, not just the models themselves. That includes computing capacity, optical networking, energy management, reliable data, security controls, and industry-specific execution. The 10 selected transactions represent more than $1.513 billion in disclosed dollar-denominated financing, plus €50 million. This is a headline transaction total, not a pure equity total: Labelbox’s financing includes a credit facility, while Skeleton’s transaction has not been fully broken down between primary investment and possible secondary share purchases. Those distinctions matter when measuring how much new capital actually enters startup balance sheets. The Macro Environment: AI Infrastructure Spending Meets a Growing Demand for Financial Discipline The latest funding activity arrives as venture investors confront an increasingly complicated AI economy. Demand for AI computing continues to grow, but the financial requirements of building and operating that infrastructure are becoming harder to ignore. GPU clusters require enormous capital commitments, substantial electricity supplies, specialized networking, and increasingly sophisticated workload-management systems. That creates opportunities for companies such as Modal, Salience Labs, and Skeleton Technologies. Each addresses a different constraint in the same market: Modal provides computing infrastructure developers can access without managing their own GPU clusters; Salience is developing optical switches to improve communication between processors; and Skeleton is building energy-storage systems designed to manage sudden fluctuations in data-center electricity demand. The distinction matters because AI infrastructure economics extend far beyond GPU prices. A data center can own expensive accelerators and still operate inefficiently because of networking bottlenecks, power fluctuations, poor utilization, or software overhead. Growing evidence also suggests public-market investors are becoming more sensitive to those costs. Shares of AI cloud provider CoreWeave fell sharply on October 14 amid concerns about borrowing costs and the sustainability of debt-financed infrastructure expansion. Financial Times reporting has also highlighted a slowdown in AI-related debt issuance as lenders become more selective. That does not mean private investors are abandoning AI infrastructure. Modal’s $750 million financing shows strong, ongoing demand for businesses that can turn compute into commercial revenue. But it suggests investors may increasingly distinguish between companies with demonstrated customer demand and infrastructure projects whose financial returns depend on uncertain future utilization. Outside computing infrastructure, OMass Therapeutics and Scimplify show that substantial capital remains available for difficult scientific and industrial problems. OMass is financing clinical development, where success ultimately depends on generating convincing evidence that experimental medicines work safely in patients. Scimplify is building a distributed manufacturing network for chemicals and critical materials, where customer qualification and production consistency determine commercial value. Those risks differ significantly from software economics. Yet both investments reflect a willingness to fund businesses whose capabilities require years of research, specialized facilities, regulatory expertise, and operating experience. The day’s enterprise software rounds introduce another important theme: AI is moving from experimentation into operational responsibility. Labelbox, Harmonic Security, Duvo, Tamr, and Dougs address different consequences of that transition, from reinforcement learning and agent execution to data accuracy, security, and regulated professional services. Together, the announcements suggest investors are looking beyond whether AI can perform a task. They increasingly want to know whether companies can deploy it reliably, measure its performance, control its risks, and generate durable revenue. Modal raises $750M in funding to expand AI infrastructure as annualized revenue run rate tops $1B San Francisco-based Modal raised $750 million in Series D financing at a $15.75 billion post-money valuation, led by Accel. Kleiner Perkins joined the investor base, while existing investors Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures participated. The financing follows a $355 million Series C announced five months earlier. Modal disclosed the latest round on October 14 alongside a major operating milestone: the company says its annualized revenue run rate has surpassed $1 billion, with usage tripling since May and year-over-year growth exceeding 15x. Founded by Erik Bernhardsson, Modal provides cloud infrastructure designed around workloads that increasingly define AI development and deployment. Its platform supports model inference, training, reinforcement learning, and isolated computing environments in which AI agents can execute code. Instead of requiring developers to manage GPU servers, container infrastructure, scheduling systems, and networking, Modal provides software interfaces that let developers allocate computing resources as needed. The company says its infrastructure spans more than 20 cloud providers. Customers include DoorDash, Cognition, Ramp, Linear, Hebbia, Runway, and companies developing robotics and drug-discovery applications. A billion-dollar run rate changes the investment case Modal’s financial milestone is important, but the terminology deserves attention. Annualized revenue run rate is not the same as annual recurring revenue. A run rate extrapolates current revenue activity into an annual figure. It does not necessarily represent contractual commitments that customers will maintain for the next 12 months. That distinction matters most for usage-based infrastructure businesses, where customer spending can fluctuate with workloads and demand. Modal also reports that its Sandboxes product, which provides isolated environments for executing code, has reached a $300 million annualized run rate. The product has become especially relevant as coding agents generate and execute more software. For investors, Modal represents a bet that the next major software infrastructure category will be built around AI workloads rather than traditional application hosting. Its competitive position depends on developer experience, workload efficiency, reliability, pricing, and the ability to manage computing capacity across different providers. However, the company faces substantial competition from established cloud platforms and specialized AI infrastructure providers. The biggest question is whether its software architecture can maintain attractive margins as customers demand lower inference costs and greater computing capacity. Funding Details Startup: Modal

Valuation: $15.75 billion post-money OMass Therapeutics raises $310M in funding to advance treatments for hormonal and autoimmune diseases Oxford-based OMass Therapeutics raised $310 million (£230 million) in an oversubscribed Series C financing, co-led by Bain Capital Life Sciences, Forbion, and Novo Holdings. Additional investors include Janus Henderson Investors, SV Health Investors, and Jefferson Life Sciences. Existing shareholders Syncona, Oxford Science Enterprises, GV, Northpond Ventures, Sanofi Ventures, British Business Bank, and the University of Oxford also participated. OMass is a biotechnology company developing small-molecule medicines for diseases involving difficult biological targets. The company originated from research conducted in Professor Dame Carol Robinson’s laboratory at the University of Oxford. Its drug-discovery platform combines native mass spectrometry, specialized biochemistry, and chemistry techniques to study proteins and their interactions in biologically relevant environments. The goal is to identify medicines that can act on targets that have historically been difficult to address. Investors are financing clinical evidence, not simply scientific discovery The largest portion of OMass’s new financing will support development of OMS1620, an experimental medicine targeting the melanocortin-2 receptor. The company is developing the drug for congenital adrenal hyperplasia and ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome, conditions involving abnormal hormone regulation. OMass plans to advance the medicine through Phase 2 clinical development. It will also use the financing to support an experimental SLC15A4 inhibitor intended for lupus and other diseases associated with abnormal immune signaling. The investment is significant because OMass is moving toward clinical milestones that could establish whether its scientific approach produces meaningful therapeutic benefits. That creates a different risk profile from AI software. A promising discovery platform can identify potential medicines, but clinical trials must establish safety and efficacy in patients. Even substantial financing cannot eliminate that uncertainty. The participation of Bain Capital Life Sciences, Forbion, Novo Holdings, and established biotechnology investors indicates confidence in the company’s pipeline and research approach. Valuation: Not disclosed What Today’s Funding Activity Reveals Today’s funding activity is notable for both its size and the diversity of problems investors are financing. Modal’s $750 million Series D accounts for nearly half of the disclosed dollar-denominated transaction total. That concentration is important. Interpreting the aggregate as evidence that every segment of the venture market is experiencing equally strong demand would be misleading. Nevertheless, the remaining rounds reveal several meaningful patterns. First, the AI infrastructure market is developing distinct investment categories. Modal operates at the computing software layer. Salience is developing photonic networking hardware. Skeleton is building energy systems to manage changes in data-center electricity demand. These companies benefit from the same broad expansion in AI computing, but their commercial models and technical risks differ considerably. Modal must manage usage-based infrastructure economics. Salience must manufacture reliable optical switches at scale. Skeleton must deliver measurable electrical performance and expand industrial production. Their presence in the same funding report illustrates how AI demand is creating opportunities across the infrastructure supply chain. Second, enterprise AI is moving toward execution and accountability. Labelbox is building training and evaluation environments. Duvo is developing agents that execute operational processes. Harmonic Security is helping businesses control employee AI usage. Tamr is improving the information those systems depend on. Dougs is combining AI automation with professional responsibility for accounting services. The emerging investment thesis is that AI’s commercial value increasingly depends on whether it can operate inside real business processes. Third, established industry relationships are becoming more important. Siemens’s investment in Skeleton provides a connection to major electrical infrastructure customers. Scimplify’s industrial investors include companies that understand its manufacturing requirements. Dougs already serves tens of thousands of businesses through a regulated professional services model. These relationships can provide distribution and operating advantages that new competitors can’t quickly reproduce. Fourth, investors remain willing to finance expensive scientific development when the opportunity is differentiated. OMass’s $310 million round shows that substantial biotech capital remains available for companies approaching important clinical milestones. Salience and Skeleton also require meaningful investment in manufacturing, testing, and engineering. Their investors are accepting technical and commercialization risks that differ from conventional software startups. Fifth, the valuation signals are selective rather than universal. Modal disclosed a $15.75 billion valuation. Skeleton crossed $1 billion. Scimplify’s reported $250 million valuation remains unconfirmed by the company. Most other startups did not disclose valuation information. That makes it difficult to infer a general change in private-market pricing from today’s announcements alone. Sixth, funding structures deserve closer attention. Labelbox’s more-than-$100-million financing combines equity and a credit facility. Skeleton’s Siemens-related investment sits alongside a disclosed secondary share transaction. Both examples show why headline transaction values should not automatically be interpreted as fresh operating capital. Finally, geographic distribution has improved under the expanded reporting period. The selected deals include companies headquartered or operating in the United States, United Kingdom, France, Estonia, and India. This does not imply that Asia experienced weak investment activity. Instead, the largest verified announcements in this 24-hour period were concentrated in North America and Europe, with Scimplify representing a significant Indian industrial investment. That is precisely why a global funding report should rank deals by significance rather than the time of day they appear. Infrastructure opportunities extend beyond GPU ownership Modal, Salience, and Skeleton address different constraints on AI computing. Their financing suggests investors see opportunities in making existing computing resources more efficient, reliable, and accessible. For founders, that opens possibilities in scheduling, networking, energy management, developer infrastructure, and specialized hardware. The important question is whether a product delivers measurable improvements in cost, reliability, or performance. 2. Revenue quality matters as much as revenue growth Modal’s reported $1 billion annualized run rate is an extraordinary operating milestone. But usage-based revenue must be evaluated differently from contractual recurring revenue. Investors should study customer concentration, workload volatility, gross margins, and how usage changes when customers optimize costs. The same principle applies to other infrastructure businesses where higher revenue can bring higher operating expenses. 3. Enterprise agents need reliable data and controls Duvo, Tamr, and Harmonic illustrate three related requirements. Agents must execute approved processes. They must use accurate information. And organizations need to control what those agents can access and do. For founders building enterprise AI, reliability and operational integration may become stronger selling points than model sophistication alone. 4. Professional accountability can become an advantage Dougs demonstrates a business model in which AI performs increasing amounts of work while qualified professionals remain responsible for the final result. That distinction may matter in accounting, legal services, healthcare administration, and other regulated industries. Founders who combine automation with trusted professional oversight may serve customers unwilling to rely entirely on autonomous systems. 5. Industrial relationships can accelerate commercialization Skeleton’s Siemens partnership and Scimplify’s investments from industrial customers provide more than financial support. They may create access to technical expertise, customer requirements, supply chains, and distribution. For deep-technology founders, an investor who can help a company manufacture and sell its product may be more valuable than one offering capital alone. 6. Biotechnology requires milestone-based financing OMass’s $310 million round provides resources to advance clinical programs rather than relying on repeated small financings during development. That approach can reduce financing interruptions, but it does not remove clinical risk. Investors should evaluate the milestones the capital is expected to finance and the evidence needed to support subsequent development. 7. AI training and evaluation are becoming separate commercial markets Labelbox’s financing indicates continued demand for the environments and feedback systems used to improve AI models. As agents handle more complicated tasks, developers need to evaluate complete workflows rather than isolated answers. The strongest companies in this category may build advantages from specialized environments, expert feedback, and long-standing relationships with AI developers. 8. Data quality can determine the value of AI investments Tamr’s business highlights an uncomfortable reality for enterprises: advanced AI models cannot compensate for consistently incorrect operating data. Founders building AI applications should account for entity resolution, record accuracy, data lineage, and system integration from the beginning. These capabilities may determine whether an agent can safely perform work in production. 9. Electricity management is becoming part of AI economics Skeleton’s financing reflects the growing importance of managing rapid changes in computing electricity demand. Data center economics depend on more than total energy consumption. Electrical stability, equipment efficiency, and the ability to use existing infrastructure effectively can influence operating costs. That creates opportunities for energy technology companies whose products improve computing performance without requiring additional generation capacity. 10. Large announced financing totals require financial interpretation Today’s rounds demonstrate why investors and journalists should separate equity, credit facilities, secondary transactions, valuation figures, and operating metrics. Those distinctions determine how much capital a company actually receives and what obligations may accompany it. They also help distinguish genuine business progress from impressive but incomplete headline figures. Conclusion October 15’s startup funding activity reveals a venture market still willing to make substantial commitments, but increasingly focused on the infrastructure and operating capabilities required to turn technology into economic value. Modal’s $750 million financing demonstrates investor confidence in AI computing infrastructure backed by significant reported usage. Salience and Skeleton are developing the networking and energy systems needed to support increasingly demanding GPU clusters. OMass shows that investors continue to finance difficult biotechnology research as programs advance toward clinical validation. Scimplify is building manufacturing capabilities in strategically important materials, while Dougs is combining AI automation with regulated professional services. Labelbox, Harmonic Security, Duvo, and Tamr are addressing another stage of AI adoption: the transition from applications that produce information to systems that perform work inside organizations. The deals differ in scale, maturity, and risk. Yet they share a common economic argument. As AI capabilities become more widely available, investors are placing substantial capital behind companies that control the infrastructure, data, industrial processes, and customer relationships required to make those capabilities useful. The next competitive advantage may come less from access to the most advanced technology and more from owning the systems that let it operate reliably, economically, and at scale. 0 Shares

data.title: Who Is Building Ground Truth for AI Agents? Top 5 best companies
data.ai_summary: Five companies—Scale AI, Keymakr, Surge AI, Labelbox, and Appen—are profiled as providers of ground truth data for AI agents. Each offers specialized platforms for labeling, RLHF, and evaluation, with Scale AI and Appen noted for large-scale projects. The article emphasizes that ground truth quality determines agent performance.
data.author: Balla

industries.name: RLHF, Human Feedback & Evaluation Data Tools
Data Quality, Validation & Ground Truth Auditing

data.full_text:
As AI agents become increasingly complex, the importance of the high-quality data they are trained on grows as well. Modern agentic systems require high-precision ground truth datasets, human feedback, response evaluation, chains of thought, and data for RLHF. This is exactly why companies engaged in data preparation and validation have become key elements of the AI ecosystem. What to look for when choosing a data provider? Before choosing a ground truth provider for AI agents, several factors should be evaluated: Quality control and verification – a reliable QA technology that combines automated algorithmic checks with multi-level human auditing.

Availability of subject matter experts – complex AI systems can only be created by people with relevant expertise.

Support for RLHF and model evaluation – modern models heavily rely on human feedback and evaluation.

Tools and integration – the ability to process large volumes of data and work with multiple languages and data types.

Security and compliance – strict adherence to GDPR, ISO/IEC 27001, and SOC 2 standards, especially if agents will work with confidential corporate data.

A combination of human expertise and automation allows maintaining both quality and speed simultaneously. Top 5 companies building ground truth for AI agents 1. Scale AI One of the most prominent giants of the industry and a key partner for leading AI laboratories (OpenAI, Meta, Microsoft). The company has built a massive ecosystem for generative AI, LLMs, autonomous systems, and next-generation agents. In addition to classic labeling, they specialize in RLHF, model testing, performance evaluation, and AI safety. Thanks to its colossal infrastructure, the company can support large-scale, ultra-complex projects. The company has its own Scale GenAI platform and a network of subject-matter experts who provide reinforcement learning and model evaluation services at an industrial scale. Best suited for: large AI companies that need millions of volumes of high-quality textual and multimodal data within tight deadlines. 2. Keymakr The company has made a powerful leap forward by offering targeted solutions specifically for agentic AI, computer vision, NLP, and complex autonomous systems. Instead of scattering efforts across standard mass labeling, they combine high-precision manual annotation from their in-house team with automated quality-control tools. A flexible approach and the ability to work with custom requirements make the company attractive to both startups and enterprise clients. Their own Keylabs platform is a powerful proprietary enterprise solution for image, video, and 3D data annotation with integrated ML automation algorithms, annotator action tracking, and multi-level QA management. They involve subject matter experts to write complex chains of thought and deploy them in RLHF. Best suited for: custom AI projects, computer vision, multimodal agents, developers of deep research systems, and robotics. 3. Surge AI A company that shifted the focus from quantity to the flawless quality of human feedback. It focuses on creating datasets for complex tasks related to logical reasoning, security, and model alignment. Thanks to this, Surge AI has become one of the key players in the field of data preparation for modern LLMs and AI agents that must operate with nuances of language and context. The platform utilizes a unique framework for adversarial testing, allowing humans to intentionally “break” models to identify vulnerabilities, alongside automated LLM-based QC bots to verify human labeling. Best suited for: RLHF tasks, building reasoning datasets, alignment tasks, and deep model evaluation. 4. Labelbox This provider offers complex software to the market. Labelbox positions itself as a full-fledged data management platform, providing clients with tools for dataset preparation, process automation, model evaluation, and the organization of human feedback within a single interface. The Labelbox platform includes modules for data management, labeling, and testing & evaluation. It allows companies to centralize their data operations. Instead of simply buying a ready-made dataset, teams get an environment where they can automate labeling with their own models and flexibly integrate both internal annotators and external crowdsourced workers. Best suited for: teams and companies seeking full control and tools to manage the entire data lifecycle and build their own AI infrastructure. 5. Appen One of the oldest, largest, and most experienced players in the global AI data market. The company’s main advantage is a colossal global network of contributors and support for hundreds of languages and dialects, allowing it to collect and annotate large-scale multilingual text, audio, and visual datasets. The Appen platform automates task distribution and quality control across a network of millions of contributors. It offers the capability to scale rapidly in geography and language. For AI agent developers, this means access to ground truth data that accounts for local cultural contexts, speech specifics, and local regulatory requirements. Best suited for: large-scale data collection, AI localization, and large multilingual projects for international markets. Who holds the keys to the autonomous future? The irony of artificial intelligence development is that the more autonomous AI agents become, the more heavily they depend on humans during their formative stage. We attempt to delegate complex work to machines – from managing investment portfolios to performing surgical operations – but the safety of this transition rests entirely on the shoulders of ground truth providers. The companies we reviewed today are literally writing the rules of the game by which the global digital economy will live tomorrow. When building your own AI agent, it is essential to consider that while the model architecture or algorithms represent the car’s chassis, the ground truth is its fuel, engine, and roadmap. And the cleanliness and expertise of this fuel will determine whether your agent reaches its destination or spins out on the very first sharp turn of the real world. Author: Balla

data.ai_summary: Labelbox raised over $100 million in Series E financing at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, led by Infinitum Partners. The company reached profitability in 2026 and serves over 400 customers, including 90% of leading U.S. AI labs. data.author: Evan Mercer
data.full_text:
Labelbox said on October 14, 2026, that it raised more than $100 million in Series E financing at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, in a round led by Infinitum Partners that combines equity with a credit facility. Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, and Snowpoint Ventures also participated, among others. Chief executive and co-founder Manu Sharma detailed the terms in a company blog post, and the company said the financing will support continued research and engineering across its two core products, Horizon and Recursion Managed Agents, as well as expansion of the teams bringing those products to customers. Sharma wrote that access to compute will be central to the company’s next chapter, noting that Infinitum’s John Yetimoglu was an early investor in Groq and is now involved in building large-scale compute infrastructure at GroqCloud. Company Position and History Labelbox stated that it reached profitability in 2026 while growing more than fivefold year over year. The company reports more than 400 customers, including over 90% of leading U.S. AI labs, and says its base spans frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Sharma, Brian, and Dan founded Labelbox in 2018. In a founder’s note, Sharma wrote that he came to the United States to learn to design and build aircraft and rockets, working on computational fluid dynamics and neural networks, and that his later roles at DroneDeploy and Planet Labs showed him how much of the opportunity in machine learning sat in data. The post describes the company’s history in three chapters: training-data software for people building AI; reinforcement-learning environments built after what Sharma calls the ChatGPT moment, when the most capable models began improving by practicing real work; and agents, which the company built for itself first before opening the system to customers. Sharma also wrote that Labelbox builds each layer of its platform itself: an agent harness designed for ultra-long-horizon agents, sandbox infrastructure that runs millions of virtual machines, its own reinforcement-learning post-training infrastructure, and an expert network of more than 4 million people. Horizon Reinforcement-Learning Environments According to the company, Horizon’s WorldSim system builds simulated companies, with code, dashboards, spreadsheets, decks, and documents filled with realistic business data, in which a model attempts a difficult multi-step task end to end while every step is recorded as a trajectory. Deterministic verifiers score each trajectory the same way on every run, and when two trajectories are both correct, an expert’s preference teaches the model what Sharma calls taste. The company describes operating at a scale of thousands of worlds and millions of graded trajectories, tuned to a lab’s pass@k targets across coding, computer use, research, multimodal, and voice work. The Horizon product page lists domains that include autonomous AI research, agent coding and software engineering, multimodal knowledge work, voice with agentic tool use, computer use, and cybersecurity. Sharma wrote that Labelbox now works with 90% of the leading frontier AI labs and hyperscalers. Recursion Managed Agents The funding announcement states that Labelbox opened Recursion Managed Agents to enterprise customers earlier in October 2026. Under the product’s design, a Managed Agent receives a goal, a trigger such as a schedule, an alert, a Slack message, a webhook, or an API call, and a rubric defining what good work looks like. A separate grader agent scores every run against the rubric line by line and points to evidence for each call; when the work misses, the agent revises it. Agents can operate in three modes: multi-agent, in which a coordinator chains specialists that each carry their own model, instructions, tools, and permissions; team, in which copies of an agent split work on a shared board and check each other’s results; and auto, the default, in which the agent decides for itself when a job needs specialists or a team. The company says agents work across more than 100 business applications and any MCP server, with every tool scoped as read only, changes data, or destructive and credentials held in a vault so the model never sees them. Sessions run in isolated sandboxes, and Labelbox says the platform runs with zero data retention at every LLM provider. Its listed compliance program covers SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, CCPA, NIST 800-171, and PCI DSS. Pricing is set per agent session hour, with compute and model spend combined in one estimate, and existing Labelbox enterprise customers receive a one-time $100 credit. Describing the company’s internal rollout in a product launch post dated October 8, 2026, Labelbox wrote, “The surprise wasn’t that agents could do the work. It was how quickly they got better at it.” The company reports running 51 agents across 11 teams, spanning software engineering, reliability, security, machine-learning research, evals, product, finance, sales, strategy, and procurement. In one internal example, Labelbox said its pull-request review agent ran 39 graded reviews on a single agent version and model, and that across the 33 reviews that passed the grader, the median cost fell from $13.15 for the first 11 reviews to $8.90 for the last 11, 32% less per review, while the agent’s memory was updated 15 times and time per review held at about 27 minutes. Under the product’s memory mechanics, once five new session reports exist, and at most once an hour, a curator agent reads them and updates the agent’s memory; customers can browse what an agent has learned and delete any lesson that no longer holds.

data.author: PR Newswire
data.full_text:
Funding will accelerate development of Horizon, which helps frontier AI labs train and evaluate models, and Recursion Managed Agents, which enables enterprises to deploy agents that improve through experience.
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Labelbox, the AI platform powering reinforcement learning for frontier models and managed agents for enterprises, today announced it has raised more than $100 million in Series E financing, including equity and a credit facility. The round was led by Infinitum Partners, with participation from Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, Snowpoint Ventures, and others.
Labelbox works with more than 400 customers, including over 90% of leading U.S. AI labs. The company reached profitability in 2026 while growing more than fivefold year over year.
As AI models become capable of performing increasingly complex tasks, the next challenge is enabling them to learn from experience and reliably execute work in real-world environments. Labelbox is addressing this opportunity through two core products: Horizon, which provides reinforcement learning environments and evaluation infrastructure for frontier AI labs, and Recursion Managed Agents, which enables enterprises to deploy fleets of agents that work inside existing business applications and improve with every run.
"Every company will soon run on AI systems that learn from their own work. Getting there takes innovation at every layer, from sandbox infrastructure and the agent harness to reinforcement learning post-training. Labelbox brings those layers together in one platform, and this funding lets us push each one further, so that frontier labs and enterprises can build AI that gets better with every run," said Manu Sharma, CEO and co-founder of Labelbox.
Advancing AI from training to execution
Horizon: Reinforcement learning for frontier AI
Horizon provides reinforcement learning environments, expert feedback, and evaluation infrastructure that help AI labs train and improve frontier models. Its environments simulate complex, multi-step work across coding, research, and other demanding tasks, enabling models to practice, receive feedback on their performance, and improve through reinforcement learning. Labelbox works with leading AI labs and hyperscalers on post-training programs.
Recursion Managed Agents: AI agents for enterprise workflows
Recursion Managed Agents enables companies to deploy fleets of AI agents inside the applications their teams already use. Agents can initiate work in response to schedules, alerts, tickets, and other triggers, coordinate across tools, and have their output evaluated against defined standards. Each run can inform the agent's memory, helping it improve how it approaches future tasks.

data.title: Amazon Mechanical Turk Will Close September 30, Shutting Down SageMaker Ground Truth Too
data.ai_summary: Amazon confirmed Tuesday that Mechanical Turk will permanently close on September 30, 2026, with workers and requesters given 35 days to migrate workflows, verify payment settings, and retrieve data. The closure also removes the MTurk Worker type from SageMaker Ground Truth and Amazon Augmented AI, ending Amazon's human data-collection infrastructure.
data.author: Jackie Manning

industries.name: Data Quality, Validation & Ground Truth Auditing

data.full_text: Amazon confirmed Tuesday that Mechanical Turk will permanently close on September 30, 2026 — giving existing requesters and workers thirty-five days to migrate workflows, verify payment settings, and retrieve any data they need before the platform goes dark. The announcement also revealed a detail buried in the MTurk FAQ closure page that the company did not spotlight: SageMaker Ground Truth and Amazon Augmented AI will close on the same date, meaning Amazon is not merely retiring one aging product but exiting the human data-collection infrastructure market entirely. The prior coverage of this story — Amazon's July announcement that it would stop accepting new customers on July 30 — documented the historical arc: a platform built on humans faking machines, consumed by machines that learned to fake humans. That story has been told. What has not been told is what the next five weeks require of the researchers, enterprise annotation teams, and workers who are still on the platform today. Amazon Is Leaving the Human-Data Market, Not Just Retiring a Product The September 30 date is not the end of one product in an otherwise intact AWS portfolio. The official closure FAQ confirms that the Amazon Mechanical Turk Worker type will no longer be available when creating SageMaker labeling jobs or Amazon Augmented AI human review workflows, also effective September 30, 2026. Amazon had positioned SageMaker Ground Truth as the managed successor to MTurk's open-crowd model. Where MTurk routed tasks to an anonymous global pool, Ground Truth used an active-learning architecture: a labeling model trained incrementally on confirmed annotations, auto-labeled the examples it could classify with high confidence, and routed only low-confidence cases to human review, cutting labeling costs by up to 70% compared to fully manual annotation. Ground Truth Plus added audit trails, confidence scores, and worker-agreement metrics — the quality management layer that MTurk's architecture never offered. That, too, is gone after September 30. Amazon's message to the market is that it has decided human-in-the-loop annotation infrastructure is not its business anymore. The annotation tier that mattered economically — the commodity layer of anonymous micro-tasks — has been automated. The managed expert layer is better served by third-party specialists. Amazon is exiting both. What the September 30 Deadline Requires The official MTurk FAQ lays out the practical logistics that affected users need to act on now: For workers: Verify payment preferences in the MTurk Worker Portal immediately. Set up a payment method and a transfer schedule in Account Settings if you have not already done so. All completed and approved HITs will be paid out on your normal disbursement schedule. Requesters can award bonuses until October 30, 2026 — thirty days past the platform's closure date. Your transaction history will remain accessible until January 28, 2027. For requesters: Verify your payment information in the MTurk Requester Portal to ensure refunds can be processed. You should expect a full refund of your pre-paid balance within thirty days of closure. HIT submission closes on September 30; any HITs submitted before that date have thirty days — until October 30 — for approval or rejection. HITs not acted on within that window will be auto-approved. Teams running active annotation pipelines should treat September 30 as the final operating day, not a soft transition point. The platform has been in maintenance mode since July, meaning no new features and minimal investment. What it offers between now and September 30 is diminishing returns on workflows that need to migrate regardless. What MTurk Built, and Why That History Now Has a Hard Endpoint Read more: Amazon Mechanical Turk Closes: AI Consumed the Platform It Was Built to Fake The machine's most consequential hour came when computer vision researcher Fei-Fei Li needed to label millions of images at a scale her team could not afford by hiring students. A chance hallway conversation at Princeton introduced her to MTurk. "He showed me the website," Li later recalled, "and I can tell you literally that day I knew the ImageNet project was going to happen." Her team crowdsourced the labeling of 3.2 million images across 5,247 categories through MTurk, producing the dataset published in 2009 that would power AlexNet's breakthrough at the 2012 ImageNet challenge and launch the deep learning era that all current AI systems descend from. MTurk later became the primary industrial channel for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — the technique that made large language models coherent enough to deploy. In this human feedback fine-tuning process, workers compare pairs of AI outputs and express preferences; a reward model trained on those preferences guides the fine-tuning of the base model. MTurk workers generated those preference pairs at scale. Their judgments — which summary was clearer, which answer more helpful, which response less harmful — were encoded into the reward models shaping ChatGPT, its predecessors, and their contemporaries. The recursive failure that ended the platform: by 2023, researchers at EPFL estimated that 33 to 46 percent of workers on an abstract summarization task were using large language models to complete their assignments and submitting the output as human judgment. The humans who were supposed to provide ground-truth signal were routing tasks through the very AI systems researchers were trying to train and evaluate. The distinction between human judgment and machine output — the platform's entire premise — had eroded from within. Who Is Replacing Amazon Mechanical Turk The data-labeling industry that absorbs MTurk's customers looks nothing like it. Analysts tracking the market describe three distinct wage tiers that have emerged as the commodity layer was automated away: At the bottom, the bulk commodity tier ran $1–$12 an hour for repetitive labeling and simple classification — this is the tier that MTurk occupied, and it has been largely absorbed by AI auto-labeling pipelines and synthetic data generation. Above it, the mid-tier holds domain professionals in finance, medicine, and law at $20–$85 an hour. At the top, credentialed PhDs and specialists command $85–$200 an hour for frontier reasoning data that current models cannot yet replicate. MTurk was built for the bottom tier. That tier no longer needs a human marketplace. Scale AI — which has partnered with major AI labs and, before Meta's $14 billion stake purchase in June 2025, was the dominant managed-annotation vendor — operates a professional annotation pipeline with domain-specialized workers and AI-assisted tooling. That stake purchase triggered departures by Google, OpenAI, and others concerned about neutrality, redirecting significant annotation volume to competitors. Mercor emerged as a primary beneficiary. The startup connects frontier AI labs with vetted experts — lawyers, doctors, engineers, PhDs — at roughly $95 an hour for specialized reasoning data, and reached $2 billion in annualized revenue as of June 2026, doubling from $760 million four months earlier. As of July 2026, Mercor was in discussions to raise approximately $500 million at $20 billion valuation — a figure that describes in one number how much capital has moved into the tier above what MTurk served. Whether that round has closed as of this writing has not been confirmed. Prolific has attracted academic and enterprise researchers who migrated from MTurk after data quality concerns mounted. The platform offers controlled participant pools with demographic targeting and IRB-compatible workflows, though it lacks MTurk's API depth at the low end. CloudResearch and Qualtrics panels offer additional academic-research alternatives. For AWS-native teams, the practical successor within Amazon's ecosystem is gone along with MTurk. Teams that need to stay in the AWS environment for compliance or integration reasons will need to evaluate managed annotation vendors with AWS Marketplace integrations, as Amazon has no announced replacement for the MTurk Worker type in SageMaker workflows after September 30. What the Closure Means for Academic Research Built on MTurk Thousands of published papers in psychology, behavioral economics, and natural language processing built their datasets through MTurk. The closure does not retroactively invalidate those studies, but the Veselovsky et al. 2023 research created an unresolved question about any MTurk-derived data collected after November 2022, when ChatGPT became publicly available. Any study that used MTurk annotation in 2023 or 2024 cannot determine from the data alone what fraction of labeled examples were produced by AI rather than human judgment. A 2025 study published in Royal Society Open Science found that MTurk workers with the platform's "master" qualification almost never missed attention checks and showed high reliability — but that non-master workers had significant quality issues. The closure removes even that option. Academic teams that have not yet migrated to Prolific or CloudResearch for IRB-compatible human-subjects research should treat the September 30 date as a hard research-design deadline. What Is Replacing Amazon Mechanical Turk? The migration path depends on the use case. For machine learning data labeling, Scale AI (Outlier), Mercor, Surge AI, and Labelbox offer vetted professional workforces with quality guarantees suited to high-stakes AI applications. For academic human-subjects research, Prolific and CloudResearch offer controlled participant pools with demographic targeting, though neither fully replicates MTurk's API flexibility at the low cost end. For basic annotation tasks, auto-labeling pipelines built on models like GPT-4o and comparable systems have largely automated the work that MTurk's commodity tier handled. For workers who earned income from MTurk, the five-week window is a soft transition rather than a hard cutoff for your existing account — but the platform has been declining for years, and the community consensus documented in worker forums is that available tasks had already collapsed. Verify your payment transfer schedule now to ensure you receive all earned wages before the platform closes. Frequently Asked Questions When does Amazon Mechanical Turk permanently close, and what should existing users do first? MTurk will permanently close on September 30, 2026. The single most important action for both workers and requesters is to verify payment settings immediately: workers should confirm a payment method and transfer schedule in the MTurk Worker Portal; requesters should verify payment information in the Requester Portal to ensure balance refunds are processed. Requesters can approve or reject HITs until October 30, 2026. Transaction history remains accessible until January 28, 2027. What else is closing on September 30 that most coverage has missed? The official MTurk FAQ confirms that the Amazon Mechanical Turk Worker type will no longer be available in SageMaker Ground Truth labeling jobs or Amazon Augmented AI human review workflows, also effective September 30, 2026. Amazon is not retiring one product — it is exiting the human data-collection infrastructure market in its entirety. Teams using SageMaker Ground Truth workflows that route to MTurk workers need to migrate those pipelines, not just their direct MTurk API integrations. Why is Amazon shutting down Mechanical Turk? Amazon has offered no public explanation beyond "careful consideration" and "an assessment." The structural reasons are visible: the commodity annotation market that MTurk occupied has been automated by AI auto-labeling pipelines, while the higher-value expert annotation market is served by managed platforms — Scale AI, Mercor, Prolific — that MTurk's open anonymous architecture was not designed to compete with. A 2023 EPFL study found that 33 to 46 percent of workers on some task types were submitting AI-generated responses as human judgment, which dissolved the platform's core value proposition. Amazon did not explain whether EU Platform Work Directive compliance obligations — which apply to microtask platforms and take effect in December 2026 — factored into the timing, though reporting from The Next Web notes the closure lands three months before that deadline. What did Amazon Mechanical Turk actually build? The most consequential output was ImageNet — the 3.2 million-image labeled dataset that computer vision researcher Fei-Fei Li's team built through MTurk crowdsourcing, published in 2009 and recognized in competition in 2012. ImageNet triggered the deep learning revolution. MTurk also supplied the human preference data underlying Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — the fine-tuning technique that aligned ChatGPT and its contemporaries with human intent. The platform that supplied the judgment to build modern AI was ultimately displaced by the AI it built.

data.title: Micro1 hits $500M run rate as AI training data gold rush accelerates
data.ai_summary: Micro1, a startup specializing in AI training data and labeling services, has reached a $500 million gross run rate, highlighting the rapid growth of the AI infrastructure sector. This milestone underscores the critical demand for high-quality human-labeled data as major tech companies race to develop more capable models amidst concerns over data scarcity. The achievement positions Micro1 competitively against rivals like Scale AI and Labelbox in the industrialized market for AI training support.
data.author: The Tech Buzz Team
data.full_text:
The race to feed AI models just hit a new milestone. Micro1, a startup specializing in AI training data and data labeling services, has reached $500 million in gross run rate, according to TechCrunch. The achievement underscores how the AI boom isn't just enriching chip makers and model developers - it's creating massive opportunities for companies that provide the fuel these systems need to learn. As OpenAI, Google, and others race to build more capable models, the infrastructure powering that development is becoming a billion-dollar business in its own right. Micro1 just became the latest proof that in the AI gold rush, selling picks and shovels can be just as lucrative as mining for gold. The startup's climb to $500 million in gross run rate represents one of the fastest growth trajectories in the AI infrastructure space, fueled almost entirely by insatiable demand for training data. The numbers tell a story about where AI development bottlenecks really exist. While Nvidia grabs headlines with GPU shortages and OpenAI dominates conversations about model capabilities, companies like Micro1 are quietly solving a less glamorous but equally critical problem: how do you generate enough high-quality, human-labeled data to actually train these models? The answer involves armies of human annotators, sophisticated quality control systems, and increasingly complex workflows for reinforcement learning from human feedback - the technique that helped make ChatGPT feel conversational. Micro1's platform connects AI companies with skilled workers who label images, rate AI responses, and provide the feedback loops that turn raw compute into useful intelligence. What makes Micro1's growth particularly striking is the timing. The company is hitting this milestone just as the industry confronts a looming shortage of quality training data. According to research from Epoch AI, we could exhaust high-quality text data for training by 2026, forcing companies to get creative about synthetic data, better labeling, and more efficient use of human feedback. That scarcity is driving up the value of platforms that can reliably deliver quality annotations at scale.

Advertisement

The competitive landscape reflects these high stakes. Scale AI, one of Micro1's chief rivals, hit a $7.3 billion valuation in 2021 and counts the Department of Defense among its clients. Companies like Labelbox, Sama, and Appen are all vying for contracts with the big AI labs. But Micro1's approach appears to be resonating - particularly its focus on reinforcement learning workflows that have become essential for training models like GPT-4 and Claude. The business model itself is revealing. Unlike pure software companies, data labeling operations blend technology platforms with managed workforces, creating gross run rates that look impressive but come with corresponding costs. Still, reaching $500 million signals that Micro1 has found a way to scale both sides of that equation effectively. For Google, Meta, Microsoft, and other companies racing to deploy AI across their product lines, reliable access to training data infrastructure has become non-negotiable. Internal teams can only scale so far. Outsourcing to specialists like Micro1 lets them move faster while maintaining the quality controls necessary for production AI systems. The growth also highlights how AI development is becoming more industrialized. Early models could be trained by small academic teams with modest budgets. Today's frontier models require coordinating thousands of labelers, managing complex feedback loops, and maintaining consistency across millions of data points. That operational complexity creates moats for companies that can execute it well.

data.title: White collar workers are getting paid $200 an hour to train AI on their jobs — but it’s not 'easy money'
data.ai_summary: White-collar professionals are being hired by AI training companies like Mercor to teach AI systems the specialized tasks they spent years mastering, with Mercor paying its network of 30,000 contractors over $4 million daily. The work pays between $50 to $350 per hour depending on expertise required, but contractors report that flat-rate gigs often consume far more hours than compensation reflects, with opaque quality assessments and no feedback on rejections. AI labs are driving demand because the largest models have already consumed most available internet text, making expert-curated training data the next critical frontier for model improvement.

Stock-Asso/Shutterstock Amanda Brown grades biology students as an assistant professor at Tarleton State University in Texas. Last summer, while she wasn't teaching, she signed up to grade an AI model's answers. What followed were tight deadlines, flat-rate gigs that swallowed far more hours than they paid for and her manager giving a verdict that her work didn't measure up, with no reasons provided. Must Read Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake — here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP Millionaires under 43 hold only 25% of their wealth in stocks. Here's where their money is actually going "It seems like easy money," Brown told The New York Times. "It really isn't." Brown is one of tens of thousands of white-collar professionals now being paid to teach AI systems the jobs they spent years learning. A July 10 Times report (1) put numbers on the trade, showing how Mercor, a San Francisco-based startup that sells training data to AI labs, pays its network of 30,000 contractors upward of $4 million every day (1). Mercor was reportedly in early talks in July that would peg its worth near $20 billion (2), according to Bloomberg. Whether the work is worth it is a harder question now, and the people doing it have started answering. What the work pays and who's buying The money sounds good. A listing on Mercor's job board offered up to $350 an hour for a psychiatry expert (3) to build clinical scenarios and check the model's answers against real medical standards, CBS News reported. Surge AI has advertised $300 to $500 an hour for management consultants and investment bankers (4), and up to $1,000 for venture capital partners. Alignerr, a Labelbox subsidiary, pays contractors with credentials like a chemistry doctorate up to $200 an hour. But most gigs pay less than that. Mercor told CBS News its roles average about $105 an hour (3), and a generalist job reviewing AI search results for errors pays $50 an hour (3). Brown herself thought that $60 an hour seemed like an attractive rate for these tasks. Who's paying for all this expertise? The AI labs are. The big models have already read most of the internet, so the next round of improvement depends on experts checking their work. That could mean, for example, a law professor grading the model's brief the way she'd grade a first-year associate's. "We are now at a stage where they need more fine-tuning and reinforcement," Christine Cruzvergara, chief education strategy officer at recruiting startup Handshake, told CBS News (3).

Story Continues

data.ai_summary: G2 published a buyer's guide evaluating eight data labeling platforms for AI and machine learning workflows, covering Roboflow, SuperAnnotate, Labelbox, Encord, Keymakr, V7 Darwin, Dataloop, and Clarifai. The article assesses each tool against criteria including annotation quality, AI-assisted labeling, multimodal data support, human-in-the-loop workflows, scalability, and MLOps integrations, drawing on G2 user reviews and satisfaction ratings. Each platform is positioned for different use cases such as computer vision workflows, enterprise-grade labeling, LLM training, multimodal annotation, and automated data labeling.

If you’ve ever spent hours cleaning datasets, fixing inconsistent annotations, or retraining models because your labels were off, you already know this: data labeling is where AI projects either take off or quietly fail. I talk to data scientists, ML engineers, and AI product teams all the time, and the frustration is consistent: labeling is slow, expensive, and painfully manual when it shouldn’t be. The bottleneck isn’t the model architecture anymore; it’s the ground truth. When I talk to ML teams, the question isn’t whether they need a platform, but which of the best data labeling tools can actually handle 10k+ annotations an hour without turning the QA process into a second full-time job. In this guide, I’ll break down the tools that actually help you label faster, maintain consistency, and plug directly into your ML pipelines, without turning your data ops into a bottleneck.
