The best data labeling tools I recommend When I think about data labeling tools, I see them as the foundation of any AI workflow. They help teams annotate and structure raw data, like text, images, video, and audio, so machine learning models can actually learn from it. What I’ve noticed over time is that they’re no longer just annotation interfaces. The better tools now handle data management, quality control, and workflow orchestration, making them a core part of the AI and MLOps lifecycle.



The best data labeling tools go far beyond basic annotation. They help you label faster, maintain consistency, and scale workflows across large, messy datasets. Data teams usually look for features like AI-assisted labeling (pre-labeling, active learning), strong collaboration and review workflows, and support for multiple data types—all paired with seamless integrations into ML pipelines through APIs and cloud infrastructure.



Where I see the biggest difference, though, is in how well these tools handle data quality and human-in-the-loop workflows. Based on G2 Data, 9 out of 10 users say data labeling software meets their requirements, with an average satisfaction rate of 91% across labeler quality, task quality, data quality, and human-in-the-loop processes. That aligns with what I hear from teams: the best tools don’t just help you annotate; they help you operationalize high-quality data at scale without slowing everything down. How did I find and evaluate the best data labeling tools? I started with G2’s category Grid report to build a shortlist of the best data labeling tools based on G2 Score, user satisfaction, and market presence. I also factored in review recency and review volume to prioritize tools with consistent, up-to-date user feedback. This helped me focus on platforms that are rated highly by real users.



Next, I analyzed G2 reviews at scale to understand what actually matters to data scientists, ML engineers, and AI teams: how well each tool handles annotation quality, where workflows break down at scale, and which platforms genuinely help teams manage labeling across different data types.



I paid close attention to feedback around usability, collaboration, automation (like AI-assisted labeling), integrations with ML pipelines, and how effectively each tool supports human-in-the-loop workflows without slowing teams down.



Since I couldn’t test these tools hands-on, I relied on insights from professionals using them daily and validated those findings against verified G2 reviews.

Roboflow: Best for computer vision workflow G2 rating: 4.8/5 ⭐ If you’re working with images or video and trying to train models for object detection, segmentation, or classification, Roboflow is the kind of tool that sits right in the middle of your workflow. Based on my research, it's more than just a data labeling software. It's a full-stack platform built specifically for computer vision teams. Roboflow brings labeling, dataset management, and iteration into one place, which is a big part of why it’s considered one of the best data labeling tools right now.



What stands out to me immediately is how much emphasis Roboflow places on speed without compromising quality. Features like Auto Label and Label Assist use foundation and custom models to dramatically reduce manual work, and in practice can significantly cut labeling time, especially for large image datasets. The Smart Polygon tool, powered by advanced segmentation models, makes annotating complex shapes significantly faster and more precise, especially when you’re working with detailed or irregular objects. This focus on usability translates well: G2 satisfaction rating for ease of use and ease of setup both sit at 94%, which aligns with the idea that teams can get up and running quickly without a steep learning curve. That’s not always a given in this category. Where I see Roboflow consistently delivers is dataset quality and human-in-the-loop workflows. Users rate features like human-in-the-loop, image segmentation, and object detection highly (around 92–93%), which makes sense given how tightly integrated the review and feedback cycles are. You can manage the entire annotation lifecycle, from assigning tasks to reviewing and approving labels, within the same interface. What stood out to me here is how well Roboflow supports team-based workflows. You can divide work across annotators, track progress in real time, and keep everyone aligned without needing external tools. Add in dataset search, analytics, and augmentation (like generating multiple variations of images), and it starts to feel less like a labeling tool and more like a system for continuously improving your training data. It’s also worth noting that the platform is widely used in industries like computer software, research, and manufacturing, which reflects its fit for both experimental and production-grade use cases. That said, based on user feedback, there are a couple of areas where teams might need to evaluate fit more closely. Pricing is one of themes I saw on some G2 reviews. Roboflow can get expensive for teams working with large datasets or requiring higher levels of automation and collaboration. Teams prioritizing speed, quality, and an all-in-one workflow find the investment justified.



I also noticed that while Roboflow is extremely strong for core computer vision workflows, some teams look for more advanced or specialized capabilities when working on highly complex labeling or custom pipelines. Still, for most computer vision teams, its focused feature set is more than enough to move quickly from raw data to production-ready models. On the whole, I’d recommend Roboflow for teams that want to move quickly from raw image data to production-ready models without juggling multiple tools along the way. What I like about Roboflow: Features like Auto Label and Smart Polygon noticeably reduce manual effort without sacrificing annotation quality.

From labeling to dataset management and review workflows, it feels like a complete system rather than a patchwork of tools. What G2 users like about Roboflow: "Roboflow provides an end-to-end pipeline for computer vision research, from dataset annotation and versioning to augmentation and model export. The interface is intuitive, and the dataset management features (splits, class balance visualization, augmentation control, and format conversion) significantly reduce experimental overhead. For academic research, the ability to quickly iterate on datasets, reproduce experiments, and export to multiple frameworks (YOLO, COCO, TensorFlow, ONNX, etc.) is extremely valuable." - Roboflow review, Abdul Rahman S. What I dislike about Roboflow: Some G2 users note that pricing can become a consideration as projects scale, especially when working with large datasets or advanced workflows but many also mention that the time savings and efficiency gains make it worthwhile.

According to G2 feedback, while Roboflow is highly effective for computer vision tasks, some users would like more advanced or customizable capabilities for specific use cases though for most teams, its focused feature set covers the essentials well. What G2 users like about Roboflow: "Some advanced features are locked behind higher pricing tiers, and large datasets can become expensive. For highly custom pipelines, there can be some limitations compared to fully self-hosted solutions." - Roboflow review, Adip D. If you're focused on the full data science and ML workflow, the DSML platforms may be worth a look. 2. SuperAnnotate: Best for enterprise-grade data labeling workflow G2 rating: 4.9/5 ⭐ SuperAnnotate stands out to me as one of the more enterprise-ready platforms for building high-quality datasets across image, video, audio, NLP, and multimodal models. It feels built for teams that care less about quick labeling wins and more about getting consistent, production-grade data at scale. One of the key strengths, according to me, is how polished and mature the platform feels, especially when it comes to usability. G2 Data backs this up strongly, with ease of use and ease of setup both sitting around 96–97%, which is unusually high for a tool this feature-rich. In practice, that means teams can onboard quickly without getting bogged down in configuration. Where SuperAnnotate really differentiates itself, though, is in how seriously it takes data quality. Features like consensus scoring, multi-step review workflows, and performance tracking for annotators are all baked into the platform, which explains why G2 users rate labeler quality, human-in-the-loop workflows, and task quality so highly (around 97–98%). It feels like the platform is designed to reduce ambiguity in labeling decisions, which is something I hear data teams struggle with all the time.



I also like how flexible it is across different data types and use cases. Whether you’re working on image segmentation, video tracking, NLP tasks like entity recognition, or even LLM fine-tuning, the platform supports it all in one place. The annotation tools themselves are highly customizable, and you can plug in your own models for pre-labeling to speed things up. Combined with AI-assisted labeling and automation, this can significantly reduce manual effort while still keeping humans in the loop for quality control. One more thing worth calling out is how well it supports team-based workflows. You can assign tasks, track annotator performance, manage multiple projects, and even tap into external annotation teams if you need to scale quickly. That level of coordination, along with integrations into cloud storage and ML pipelines, makes it easier to turn labeling into a repeatable, scalable process rather than a one-off task. At the same time, some users mention that because the platform is so feature-rich, it can take a bit of time to fully understand and make the most of all its advanced capabilities, especially for teams that are newer to structured data labeling workflows. Even so, once teams get familiar with the system, many find that the depth actually becomes a strength rather than a barrier. The next theme I noticed in G2 feedback is performance at scale. Some users mention that when working with very large datasets or more complex projects, the platform can occasionally feel slower or less responsive. It’s not something that shows up in smaller workflows, but it’s worth considering if you’re handling high-volume annotation operations. For most teams, the overall functionality and depth of the platform still outweigh these occasional slowdowns. Overall, I’d recommend SuperAnnotate to teams that are looking to move beyond basic labeling and build a scalable, quality-first data operation. If you’re managing multiple annotators, working across different data types, or need tight control over quality and workflows, this is one of the best data labeling tools to consider. It's usability scores are high on G2, and once workflows are set up, SuperAnnotate feels efficient to navigate and manage projects.

Features like multi-step review workflows, consensus scoring, and annotator performance tracking make it easier to maintain consistency across large teams. What G2 users like about SuperAnnotate: "What I like most about SuperAnnotate is how easy it is to use. The interface feels clean and straightforward, so I can focus on the actual annotation instead of figuring out tools. I also like that it makes organizing tasks and reviewing work simple, which helps me stay efficient and accurate. Overall, it makes annotation work smoother, less stressful, and more productive compared to many other platforms." - SuperAnnotate review, Miriam O. What I dislike about SuperAnnotate: Some G2 users mention that performance can slow down when working with very large datasets or more complex projects, though this tends to show up more at scale than in smaller workflows.

According to G2 feedback, there can be a learning curve when getting started, especially when setting up workflows or managing more advanced features—but that complexity also reflects the level of control the platform offers. What G2 users dislike about SuperAnnotate: "There isn't much to dislike, but if I had to point out something, it would be the initial learning curve. Because there are so many advanced features, it takes a little bit of time to get fully comfortable with the workspace. Also, the browser can occasionally lag slightly if you are working with a massive batch of ultra-high-resolution images, but it's rarely a major issue."

- SuperAnnotate review, Mohammed Z 3. Labelbox: Best for LLM training and GenAI model evaluation G2 rating: 4.5/5 ⭐ Labelbox sits at an interesting intersection: it's less a traditional labeling tool and more of a platform where annotation, model-assisted labeling, and data management come together in one place. Based on what I've seen in G2 reviews, it's particularly well-suited for teams building LLM training pipelines and supervised ML workflows. What stands out most from user feedback is how clean and navigable the interface is. Reviews consistently call out the dashboard, keyboard shortcuts, and annotation workspace as genuinely easy to work with, even for newer annotators joining a project mid-stream. Features like model-assisted labeling and auto-annotation are a recurring highlight, with users noting how much time they save on repetitive tagging, particularly for large image and text datasets. The Python SDK and GraphQL API support also come up frequently in reviews from ML engineers. The ability to plug Labelbox directly into training pipelines, uploading assets, triggering labeling tasks, and pulling annotations back out programmatically, is clearly a draw for more technical teams that don't want their data pipeline to stop at the annotation interface. Where Labelbox has moved ahead of most tools in this category is in its GenAI and LLM evaluation capabilities. Beyond standard annotation, the platform now supports multimodal chat evaluations, side-by-side model comparisons, and LLM-as-a-judge workflows — which means teams can use the same platform to both create training data and evaluate model outputs. For teams working on RLHF, fine-tuning, or prompt optimization, that kind of end-to-end setup removes a significant handoff between tooling. On G2, Labelbox scores above category average on data quality, labeler quality, and named entity recognition — all sitting at 91–92% against a category average of 91% — which lines up with what users describe in reviews: consistent output and reliable annotation across text-heavy workflows. What I also like is how well Labelbox handles team coordination. You can assign tasks, track annotator progress, and monitor time spent per label from the dashboard, which removes the need for a separate project management layer.

The platform also supports active learning workflows, where model predictions feed back into the labeling queue to prioritize the most uncertain samples. In practice, that means teams get more signal out of each labeling cycle rather than annotating randomly. There are some nuances to consider based on G2 feedback I saw. While Labelbox is built for large datasets, that scale can occasionally come at a cost. Some users mention the platform slows down when processing very large datasets, which is more noticeable in high-volume workflows than smaller projects. For most teams, the time saved through automation and model-assisted labeling still outweighs the occasional lag. Also getting fully comfortable with Labelbox's built-in tools takes some ramp-up time, especially for annotators who are newer to structured labeling platforms. Once past the initial curve though, the depth of the toolset is exactly what makes it effective for complex, production-grade workflows. If you're building LLM training pipelines or running active learning workflows at scale, Labelbox is worth a serious look in my opinion. It's the kind of platform that earns its place when annotation needs to connect tightly to model training, not just sit upstream of it. What I like about Labelbox:

The dashboard makes team coordination straightforward. You can assign tasks, track annotator progress, and monitor time per label without needing a separate project management tool.

Active learning support means model predictions feed back into the labeling queue automatically, so teams prioritize the right data rather than annotating at random. What G2 users like about Labelbox: "I like how Labelbox helps it's users by giving them a simple and better label data within short time. It contains a vast variety of tools that are simple and saves a lot of time while working as a team. t's organised data helps in making a better prompt while working with AI models." - Labelbox review, Siva Kamal P. What I dislike about Labelbox: Based on G2 reviews, processing large datasets can slow the platform down, which tends to show up most in high-volume workflows — though the automation features generally offset the wait.

Another thing to consider is the learning curve with the built-in toolset, particularly for newer annotators but like other tools on the list once past the initial ramp-up, the depth of the platform becomes an asset rather than a barrier. What G2 users dislike about Labelbox: "If you are working on a large data sets, you might feel it a bit slower as it takes time to process. And it's not a beginner user friendly, it requires bit experience to explore and work with inbuilt tools."

- Labelbox review, Ramu K 4. Encord: Best for multimodal data annotation G2 rating: 4.8/5 ⭐ If you’re working with video, audio, text, any multimodal data, or even medical imaging, Encord feels like a step up from traditional labeling tools. It’s designed to manage the entire AI data lifecycle, not just annotation, but also curation, automation, and evaluation. One thing I keep coming back to with Encord is how deeply it’s built around multimodal and AI-assisted workflows. You can work across text, video, audio, LiDAR, and even medical imaging in one environment. That’s a big advantage for teams building more advanced models. The ability to plug in foundation models like GPT, Gemini, or your own models into the labeling pipeline also changes how quickly you can move. Instead of starting from scratch, you’re layering automation on top of human review, which is where most data teams are heading. From a usability standpoint, the G2 Data shows a strong balance between capability and accessibility. Ease of use and ease of setup both land in the low-to-mid 90s (around 93–94%), which suggests teams aren’t hitting major friction when getting started, even with the platform’s depth. I also noticed strong scores for ease of admin, ease of doing business, and quality of support, which usually indicates that the platform works well not just technically, but also from an onboarding and ongoing support perspective. That’s especially important for teams managing larger annotation operations. Where Encord starts to pull ahead is in how it approaches data quality and workflow customization. Features like human-in-the-loop workflows, image segmentation, and object detection are rated highly (around 92–93%), and that reflects how configurable the system is. You can build multi-stage review pipelines, define detailed ontologies, and track annotator performance in real time. Rather than forcing you into a fixed workflow, it gives you the flexibility to shape processes around your use case. With built-in analytics and dataset insights layered in, teams get much better visibility into how labeling quality evolves over time. It’s also worth noting how broadly Encord is used across industries like computer software, research, higher education, and manufacturing. That tells me it’s flexible enough to support both experimental AI work and more operational, production-grade use cases. In more recent G2 feedback, one theme that comes up is the pace of feature updates. Encord ships improvements frequently, which can require teams to stay more closely aligned with evolving workflows. That said, users consistently highlight the customer success team for helping them stay aligned and get the most out of new features. I also came across feedback around video analysis capabilities. While frame-by-frame annotation is strong, there’s interest in more advanced functionality for analyzing full video clips. Even so, this hasn’t limited teams’ ability to work effectively on the platform, and it’s an area the Encord team appears to be actively improving. All things considered, if you’re working with multimodal data or anything more complex than straightforward annotation, Encord is worth a closer look. It’s the kind of platform that starts to make sense once your workflows get messy and you need more control over how everything is labeled and reviewed. From what I’ve seen, it really clicks for teams dealing with large, complex datasets where structure, flexibility, and automation all need to work together. What I like about Encord: Encord handles multimodal data well. You can work across video, images, text, audio, and even more complex formats like DICOM or LiDAR in one place, which makes it easier to manage advanced AI workflows.

Features like customizable ontologies, multi-stage reviews, and real-time analytics make it easier to maintain data quality as projects scale. What G2 users like about Encord: "We build a lot of infrastructure in-house, but made a strategic decision to use best-in-class tools that Encord offers for training data curation and annotation. The S3 integration works really well - we connected our AWS pipeline and now data just flows where it needs to go. Our team can pull up everything in Encord to review and annotate without any problems. The interface is intuitive and AI features like SAM integration save us a lot of time. The whole workflow from ingestion to export is smooth, which matters when you move fast. When we do hit issues, their support team is quick to respond through Slack." - Encord review, Brian E. What I dislike about Encord: In recent G2 feedback, I noticed that frequent feature updates mean teams may need to spend a bit more time staying aligned with evolving workflows, though users often highlight the support team for helping with that.

Based on a G2 review, teams working on more advanced video use cases may look for additional functionality to analyze full clips, though the existing tools are sufficient for many workflows.Users still note that frame-by-frame annotation for videos is strong. What G2 users dislike about Encord: "It would be helpful to have more functionality for analyzing video clips, in addition to the existing tools for frame-by-frame analysis. That said, this has not hindered our ability to work on the platform and is already on the Encord team's radar." - Encord review, Angela S. 5. Keymakr: Best for managed computer vision annotation with human expertise G2 rating: 4.8/5 ⭐ Keymakr occupies a different position in this list compared to the other tools in this list. Rather than leading with a self-serve platform, it operates as a managed annotation service backed by its own proprietary tooling — an in-house team of skilled annotators paired with a four-level QA system that combines human oversight with automation. For teams that don't want to manage an annotation workforce in-house, that setup removes a significant operational burden. The annotation work is supported by Keylabs, Keymakr's proprietary platform, which was originally built for internal use, meaning usability and quality were the primary design constraints rather than feature breadth. That origin shows up in how I see reviewers describe working with it: straightforward to get started on, with tools that feel built for annotators rather than platform architects. What stands out most consistently across G2 reviews is the quality of communication and the partnership-oriented approach. Reviewers across small businesses, mid-market, and enterprise segments describe a team that checks in proactively, asks clarifying questions before starting batches, and course-corrects quickly based on feedback. Several users specifically mention the pilot study model, where Keymakr runs a small sample before committing to the full project, as something that builds confidence early and catches misalignment before it compounds. The Keylabs platform supports simultaneous work across 50+ annotators without loss of productivity, which matters when projects need to scale quickly. Annotation types span bounding boxes, polygons, semantic segmentation, keypoint annotation, LiDAR point clouds, and frame-by-frame video annotation, covering the full range of computer vision use cases from ADAS and robotics to medical imaging and industrial automation. Where reviews get more nuanced is around two things. The platform UI comes up occasionally. Some users mention the intiial setup and navigation can take some time to get used to. That said, once teams find their footing, the review interface does what it needs to do without getting in the way of the work. A few reviewers also note that getting to the right output requires regular feedback sessions, especially in early project stages. That's not a flaw so much as a characteristic of how the service model works and most teams find that the upfront investment in alignment pays off in fewer corrections and more consistent output down the line. Overall, if your bottleneck is finding reliable annotators rather than building annotation infrastructure, I'd recommend Keymakr. It's one of the few tools in this list where the service is the product — and for teams that need high-quality computer vision annotations delivered rather than a platform to do it themselves, that distinction matters. What I like about Keymakr: The managed service model means teams get high-quality annotations without building and managing an annotator workforce. The pilot study approach in particular makes it easy to validate quality before committing to a full project.

The Keylabs platform enables large annotation teams to work simultaneously at scale, and the four-level QA system means quality control is baked into the process rather than left to the client What G2 users like about Keymakr: "I like the fact that Keymakr integrates seamlessly with our build process and our automated labeling pipeline. It generally fits well with all of our workflows, allowing us to streamline the labeling process efficiently. This integration capability is crucial for maintaining our overall productivity and ensuring that our data labeling tasks proceed smoothly without any interruptions. Keymakr’s compatibility with our existing systems means fewer headaches and a smoother operation overall, which is incredibly valuable for our team." - Keymakr review, Eric V. What I dislike about Keymakr: Based on G2 reviews, the initial setup and navigation take some time to get used to like any other data labeling software but once teams are familiar with the interface, the workflow becomes more straightforward and doesn't get in the way of the actual annotation work.

Some users note that customized projects require consistent client involvement, especially early on. Most find that the back-and-forth pays off in fewer corrections and more consistent output over time. What G2 users dislike about Keymakr: "Some mistakes are repetitive. Additionally, the initial setup took some time to adjust, although it became straightforward after that period." - Keymakr review, Rinat L. 6. V7 Darwin: Best for pixel-perfect computer vision annotation G2 rating: 4.8/5 ⭐ V7 Darwin is a purpose-built annotation platform for computer vision teams that need precision, speed, and workflow control in one place. Based on G2 reviews I saw, it's particularly well-regarded among teams working on complex segmentation tasks, medical imaging, and video annotation — and it's used broadly across research, healthcare, industrial automation, and software companies. What comes through most consistently in reviews is how much the annotation interface itself stands out. The Auto-Annotate tool, powered by segment anything model (SAM) and other foundation models, is mentioned repeatedly as a genuine productivity multiplier. The subtract and merge tools for pixel-perfect polygon labeling also come up frequently in reviews. Combined with keyboard shortcuts that cover almost every action, the interface feels built for annotators who are moving fast through large datasets. Video annotation is another area where V7 Darwin consistently pulls ahead. The interpolation feature tracks objects across frames automatically, with several reviewers noting it cuts per-task time by close to half. For teams working with multi-camera views or long video sequences, that's a meaningful efficiency gain that compounds across a project. The platform also handles medical imaging well, supporting DICOM, NIfTI, and whole slide image annotation with MPR and 3D rendering, which explains the strong representation of healthcare and research users in the review base. That depth of format support makes it one of the more versatile tools in this list for specialized or domain-specific use cases. Customer support responsiveness is a recurring highlight I saw, with multiple reviewers describing a team that ships feature requests quickly and stays engaged throughout projects. Based on G2 reviews, teams working with large volume of datasets might see a occasional platform lag though it's worth noting this is a pattern that shows up across most data labeling platforms at scale, not specific to V7 Darwin. Multiple reviewers also note that it doesn't get in the way of the core annotation experience. Also, teams with growing projects may find dataset navigation and filtering slightly less intuitive as file volumes increase but most users note that it remains a minor friction point rather than a blocker and many highlight that V7 actively takes feedback on board and works quickly to improve the experience. If you're building computer vision models and need annotation tooling that keeps up with complex tasks without slowing your team down, V7 Darwin is one of the strongest options in this category in my view. It clicks especially well for teams doing segmentation, video tracking, or medical imaging work where precision and speed both matter. What I like about V7 Darwin: The Auto-Annotate tool and interpolation feature genuinely reduce annotation time on complex tasks — the kind of improvement that shows up not just in demos but consistently across real user workflows.

Medical imaging support across DICOM, NIfTI, and WSI formats makes it one of the few tools in this category that handles specialized domain annotation without requiring a separate tool. What G2 users like about V7 Darwin: "Video annotation is very easy and its predictive labeling tool is really easy to use. We are able to annotate massive datasets to train our ML models." - V7 Darwin review, Jed D. What I dislike about V7 Darwin: Based on G2 reviews, teams working with large volumes of data may see occasional platform lag, which worth considering for high-volume projects, though most reviewers note it doesn't affect output quality or the core annotation experience

A few users on G2 observe that dataset navigation and filtering can feel less intuitive as file volumes grow — a consideration for teams managing large, complex projects, though most users find it a minor friction point. What G2 users dislike about V7 Darwin: "While it is robust, it can sometimes feel slightly complex to navigate, especially when dealing with advanced features. Certain modules could be more intuitive and user-friendly, as new users may require extra time to adapt. Additionally, occasional lag in system responsiveness was noticeable during peak usage" - V7 Darwin review, Shiv S. 7. Dataloop: Best for data management G2 rating: 4.4/5 ⭐ Dataloop stands out for how it approaches data management across the AI lifecycle. Rather than focusing only on annotation, it’s built to organize, version, and move data through different stages of development in a structured way.



What I like about Dataloop is how it treats data as something that needs to be continuously managed and improved. It gives you more control over how datasets are structured, updated, and connected to model performance over time, which becomes increasingly important as projects scale. Another key strength is how flexible Dataloop is when it comes to handling different data types and workflows. G2 Data reflects this pretty clearly, with data types, object detection, and image segmentation all scoring highly (around 93–94%). It’s designed to support a range of use cases, whether you’re working with images, video, or structured data, and that flexibility shows up in how you can configure pipelines. Dataloop is strong in automation too. The platform leans into AI-assisted labeling and pipeline automation, which can help reduce manual effort and speed up iteration cycles. Instead of treating labeling as a standalone task, it integrates it into a broader system where models, data, and workflows continuously interact. For teams working on production AI systems, that kind of setup can make a real difference in how quickly you move from raw data to usable outputs. Another thing I noticed is how well Dataloop handles dataset versioning and traceability. It makes it easier to track changes over time, which is critical when you're iterating on models and need to maintain data quality. I also like how tightly Dataloop connects data, models, and pipelines. That integration makes feedback loops faster, so teams can iterate more quickly without constantly switching between tools. From a usability perspective, the G2 Data shows a fairly balanced picture. Ease of use and setup sit around the high 80s to 90%, which suggests the platform is accessible but still carries some depth. I see that reflected in how Dataloop is designed: it’s not overly simplified, and some users note it take time to learn but on the flip side it gives teams the ability to manage more complex workflows as they grow. Another nuance that comes up in G2 feedback is performance at scale. Some users mention that when working with very large datasets or more complex pipelines, teams may notice differences in responsiveness depending on workload. This is more noticeable in high-volume scenarios, but for many teams, the platform’s flexibility and data management capabilities still make it a strong fit for scaling AI workflows.

Irrespective of these considerations, if your data is getting harder to manage and your projects are scaling in complexity, I'd point you to Dataloop. It's the kind of platform that gets more useful the bigger your operation gets. What I like about Dataloop: Dataloop gives you more control over how datasets are organized, versioned, and connected to model workflows as things evolve.

Features like object detection, image segmentation, and data handling are rated highly, which shows in how easily you can adapt it to different use cases. What G2 users like about Dataloop: "DataLoop excels at constructing quality data infrastructure for unstructured data, streamlining computer-vision pipelines, and ensuring seamless integration with robust security measures. A reliable ally in modern data management."

- Dataloop review, George M. What I dislike about Dataloop: Some G2 users mention that it can take time to get fully comfortable with how workflows and pipelines are structured, reflecting the platform’s depth and complexity.

I also came across feedback around performance at scale. When working with very large datasets, performance may vary slightly depending on project complexity, though the platform’s flexibility and data management capabilities continue to support most use cases effectively. What G2 users dislike about Dataloop: "Sometimes tools get stuck and need to be reopened for a smooth experience." - Dataloop review, Deep A. 8. Clarifai: Best for automated data labeling and model development G2 rating: 4.3/5 ⭐ If there’s one thing Clarifai tries to do, it’s live up to its name — clarify how you build and scale AI data workflows. Based on my research, it leans less toward being a traditional labeling tool and more toward acting as a broader AI platform where labeling, model development, and data management all come together. It’s especially relevant for teams that want to automate as much of the data pipeline as possible rather than rely heavily on manual annotation.



A big part of that comes down to how deeply it integrates AI into the labeling process. Clarifai pushes hard on automation, with features like auto-labeling, semi-supervised annotation, and one-click model training. The idea is pretty straightforward: instead of spending weeks labeling data manually, you let models handle a significant portion of the workload and then layer human review on top. From a practical standpoint, that can drastically reduce labeling time and cost, especially for teams dealing with large-scale datasets. It also helps that the platform supports a range of data types like images, video, and text, so you’re not locked into a single modality.In fact, its strongest capabilities are in image and video recognition, object detection, facial recognition, visual search, text and audio processing (NLP, speech). It’s particularly strong when working with unstructured data.



Looking at G2 Data, users highlight strengths in areas like data types, object detection, and image segmentation, all scoring in the 90s. That lines up with how flexible the platform feels when working across different use cases. Ease of use and ease of setup land around the high 80s to 90%. I also noticed strong scores around quality of support, which is important for a tool that sits closer to the infrastructure layer than a simple annotation interface.



One more aspect I find interesting is how Clarifai approaches data management. Features like vector search, dataset versioning, and embedding-based indexing make it easier to organize and retrieve data as projects grow. Instead of treating datasets as static, it allows teams to continuously refine and explore them, which becomes increasingly important once you’re working with millions of data points. Combined with integrations across frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow, it feels well-suited for teams that want to connect labeling directly with model training and deployment. Some G2 users note that pricing can become a consideration, especially as usage scales across larger datasets or more advanced workflows. For teams leveraging its automation and end-to-end capabilities, the overall value often aligns well with the investment.



I also came across feedback around documentation, particularly for newer users getting started with the platform. While the available resources cover the core functionality, some teams would benefit from more beginner-friendly guidance. but once familiar, many users are able to take full advantage of the platform’s depth and flexibility. Taking everything into account, Clarifai starts to make a lot of sense if you’re trying to move fast and don’t want to juggle separate tools for labeling, training, and deployment based on what I've seen. It’s especially useful for startups and developer-led teams that want to build and ship AI features quickly, with automation doing a good chunk of the heavy lifting. What I like about Clarifai: Features like auto-labeling and AI-assisted workflows make it easier to reduce manual effort and move faster, especially with large datasets.

Clarifai's flexibility when it comes to labeling types is a key strength. It can handle everything from simple classification to bounding boxes, segmentation, and even video tracking in one place, which makes it easier to work across different AI use cases. What G2 users like about Clarifai: "Clarifai offers some of the most pre-built (OOTB) models for many application scenarios, which provide accurate and fast tagging results.



The creation of one's own models to recognize special requirements, on the other hand, is easily possible through an intuitive UI and can be learned by anyone. The models, also combined with workflows, can be very easily integrated and used in our Online Media Net (OMN) application so that computer vision can frequently be used with a high number of images directly from our application. We also have good experience with performance and customer support." - Clarifai review, Oliver B. What I dislike about Clarifai: Some G2 users observe that pricing can become a consideration for smaller teams as projects scale, especially for teams working with larger datasets or more advanced use cases. But for many, the automation and time savings help justify the investment.

I also came across feedback around documentation, where newer users may look for more beginner-friendly guidance when getting started, though once familiar, teams are able to make full use of the platform’s capabilities. What G2 users like about Clarifai: "Despite its strengths, Clarifai does come with some challenges. The pricing structure can be prohibitive for small businesses or individual developers, as it feels more aligned with enterprise-level budgets. Furthermore, while the platform offers extensive features, the documentation can sometimes lack depth, leaving users searching for external resources or support." - Clarifai review, Verified G2 user. Kili: Best for collaborative data annotation with strong governance Best data labeling tools: Frequently asked questions (FAQs) Got more questions? G2 has the answers! Q1. What is the best data labeling platform for a small AI startup on a tight budget? If you’re a small AI startup watching costs closely, Roboflow, SuperAnnotate, and V7 Darwin are some the best data labeling platform for startups to look at. These platforms tend to appeal to lean teams because they combine annotation workflows with automation features that help reduce manual effort. Roboflow is especially appealing for startups that want dataset management and computer vision workflows in one place, while SuperAnnotate and V7 Darwin can work well for teams that need room to grow without jumping into overly complex enterprise tooling on day one. Q2. What does “data labeling stuff” actually include? Data labeling includes the tools and workflows used to tag raw data so machine learning models can learn from it. That can mean annotating images with bounding boxes, segmenting objects in video, tagging text for NLP tasks, labeling audio, or reviewing model-generated predictions. Most modern data labeling platforms also include automation, quality assurance workflows, collaboration features, and dataset management, so it’s not just about drawing boxes anymore. Q3. What is the easiest data labeling software for a team that’s not super technical? If ease of use is your top priority, Labelbox, Dataloop, and SuperAnnotate are good places to start. These tools are generally easier for non-technical teams to navigate because they offer cleaner interfaces, guided workflows, and less setup overhead than more engineering-heavy options. V7 Darwin is also worth considering if you want an annotation experience that feels modern and automation-first without requiring your team to manage a highly technical stack. Q4. Which data labeling platform is the most cost-effective while still offering good automation? For teams that want to keep costs down without giving up automation, Roboflow, Dataloop, and SuperAnnotate stand out. These platforms can help reduce annotation time through AI-assisted labeling, pre-labeling, and workflow automation, which matters if your team is trying to do more with fewer people. The most cost-effective choice usually comes down to how much automation you actually use, since the right platform can lower labeling costs by speeding up repetitive tasks and reducing rework. Q5. What is the most scalable data labeling solution for an enterprise ML pipeline? For enterprise-scale machine learning pipelines, Encord, SuperAnnotate, and Labelbox are often the strongest fits. These platforms are better suited for high-volume annotation programs because they support large datasets, team-based workflows, governance controls, and more advanced quality management. If your organization is working across multiple data types or large model training cycles, these tools tend to be better positioned to support that complexity than startup-focused platforms. Q6. Which data labeling SaaS tools have strong QA and workforce management built in? If quality assurance and workforce coordination are major priorities, SuperAnnotate, Labelbox, and Encord are strong candidates. These platforms are better equipped for structured review pipelines, role-based workflows, and performance oversight, which helps teams maintain label consistency at scale. They’re especially useful when multiple annotators, reviewers, and project owners need to work together without losing control over quality. Q7. What’s the go-to data labeling tool for teams using PyTorch and TensorFlow? For teams building with PyTorch and TensorFlow, Roboflow, Labelbox, and Encord are common choices because they fit well into modern ML workflows. The main reason is not that they replace your framework, but that they make it easier to prepare, manage, and export training data in formats your models can use. If you want smoother handoffs between annotation and model training, these platforms are usually good starting points. Q8. What is the most reliable data labeling software for training computer vision models? For computer vision, reliability usually comes down to annotation quality, support for complex image and video tasks, and strong review workflows. Encord, Roboflow, and V7 Darwin are all strong contenders here. Roboflow is often attractive for teams focused on end-to-end vision workflows, while Encord and V7 Darwin are well suited for teams that need more advanced annotation depth and tighter quality controls for production-grade datasets. Q9. Which companies offer the best all-in-one data labeling platforms for autonomous driving datasets? For autonomous driving use cases, Encord, SuperAnnotate, and Labelbox are among the strongest all-in-one platforms to evaluate. These projects usually demand support for large-scale image and video annotation, complex object tracking, and tightly managed QA workflows. If your team is working with autonomous driving datasets, you’ll usually want a platform that can handle scale, precision, and collaboration rather than a lightweight point solution. Q10. Which data annotation tools give the highest-quality labels for NLP projects? For NLP projects, Labelbox, Dataloop, Taskmonk, and Clarifai are worth considering. High-quality NLP labeling depends a lot on workflow design, reviewer oversight, and consistency across annotators, so the best tools are the ones that make those controls easier to manage. If your use case involves text classification, entity extraction, or more nuanced language tasks, these platforms can be strong options depending on how much human review and process control your team needs. Label it like it is After looking at all these tools side by side, one thing became pretty clear to me: data labeling is no longer just about annotation nowadays. It’s about how well you manage, scale, and trust your data over time. The best tools are competing on how well they help you build systems around your data, whether that’s automation, quality control, or integrating directly into your ML workflows.



What also stood out to me is that there’s no single “best” tool for everyone. Some platforms are built for speed and computer vision workflows, others for enterprise-grade quality control, and some for managing complex, multimodal datasets. The right choice really comes down to where you are in your AI journey, whether you’re just getting started with labeling or trying to operationalize data at scale.



If there’s one takeaway I’d leave you with, it’s this: the quality of your model will never outpace the quality of your data, and your tooling plays a huge role in that. Choosing the right data labeling platform isn’t just a tooling decision; it’s a foundation for everything you build on top of it.



If you’re exploring the next step beyond labeling, I’d also recommend checking out my guide on the best machine learning tools to see how these platforms fit into the broader AI stack.

data.full_text:
Every enterprise AI deployment, from the simplest classifier to the most complex agentic system, depends on infrastructure. The CEOs building that infrastructure are, in many ways, building the foundation of the entire AI economy. From GPU clouds and model serving platforms to vector databases and data observability, these leaders are defining how organizations train, deploy, monitor, and scale AI in production. Companies are listed in alphabetical order. This list is non-exhaustive. 1. Anyscale: Keerti Melkote, CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: ~$281M Keerti Melkote took the CEO role at Anyscale in 2024, bringing enterprise-building experience from founding Aruba Networks (acquired by HPE for $3B). Anyscale provides a distributed AI computing platform built on the open-source Ray framework, enabling enterprises to scale AI workloads across clusters with simplified development and deployment, a layer that has become essential as AI workloads grow beyond what single machines can handle. Under Melkote’s leadership, Anyscale has grown 4x in revenue year-over-year and partnered with Microsoft to deliver AI-native computing on Azure. The Ray framework has become the de facto standard for distributed AI at scale, powering workloads at major AI labs including OpenAI. Melkote’s mandate is to translate that open-source adoption into enterprise revenue, a playbook he executed successfully at Aruba. 2. Baseten: Tuhin Srivastava, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: ~$585M | Valuation: $5B Tuhin Srivastava co-founded Baseten to solve what he saw as the critical bottleneck in enterprise AI: getting models from research into production reliably and at scale. Baseten’s inference platform provides serverless infrastructure for deploying, managing, and scaling ML models across multiple clouds with automatic scaling, positioning the company as what some have called “the AWS of AI inference.” Baseten raised a $300M Series E in January 2026 from IVP, CapitalG, and NVIDIA, reaching a $5B valuation. Srivastava has built the company into one of the fastest-growing AI infrastructure providers by focusing relentlessly on inference performance and developer experience, two areas where enterprises are increasingly willing to pay a premium as AI moves from experimentation to mission-critical production workloads. 3. CoreWeave: Michael Intrator, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: Jersey City, NJ | Total Funding: $200M+ equity (plus $2B NVIDIA investment in Class A stock) | NASDAQ: CRWV Michael Intrator co-founded CoreWeave as a purpose-built AI cloud platform and has scaled it into one of the most important GPU infrastructure providers in the world. CoreWeave operates 40+ data centers globally, offering optimized NVIDIA GPU clusters with ultra-low-latency networking and committed power capacity designed specifically for AI training and inference, a specialization that general-purpose cloud providers struggle to match. Intrator announced plans to deploy NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and build 5+ gigawatts of AI factory capacity by 2030, numbers that put CoreWeave in the same infrastructure conversation as the hyperscalers. The company’s deep strategic partnership with NVIDIA and its focus on purpose-built AI compute have made it a primary infrastructure provider for enterprises and AI labs that need guaranteed GPU capacity. 4. Databricks: Ali Ghodsi, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: $5B+ | Valuation: $134B (February 2026) Ali Ghodsi co-founded Databricks with the creators of Apache Spark and has built it into the most valuable private AI company in the world. The Databricks Lakehouse Platform unifies data warehousing and data lakes with ML training, feature engineering, and AI-native capabilities, providing enterprises with a single platform for data and AI workloads that replaces what used to require a dozen different tools. Databricks surpassed $5.4 billion in ARR in Q1 2026 with 65% year-over-year growth, raised a $5B Series F at a $134B valuation, and is preparing for what would be one of the largest technology IPOs in history. Ghodsi’s acquisition of Tecton (feature store) in August 2025 signaled Databricks’ intent to own the entire ML infrastructure stack. His combination of academic pedigree (UC Berkeley professor), open-source community leadership, and enterprise sales execution has made Databricks the reference platform for enterprise AI. 5. Datadog: Olivier Pomel, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: New York, NY | NASDAQ: DDOG | Market Cap: ~$26B+ Olivier Pomel co-founded Datadog as an infrastructure monitoring platform and has expanded it into the comprehensive observability layer that enterprises use to monitor everything, including their AI systems. Datadog provides visibility into ML model performance, data quality, and infrastructure health across production AI pipelines, integrating with the ML tools and frameworks that data science teams already use. As AI moves from experimentation to production, the need to monitor model behavior, detect drift, and ensure reliability becomes mission-critical, and Datadog’s existing presence in enterprise infrastructure gives it a natural wedge into AI observability. Pomel has built a public company with $26B+ in market cap by consistently expanding the platform’s scope, and AI infrastructure monitoring represents one of Datadog’s largest growth vectors for the next era. 6. Fireworks AI: Lin Qiao, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: Redwood City, CA | Total Funding: ~$327M | Valuation: $4B Lin Qiao co-founded Fireworks AI after working on the PyTorch framework at Meta, experience that gave her deep insight into what enterprises need from AI inference infrastructure. Fireworks provides an optimized platform for serving large language models and generative AI applications with low latency and high throughput, offering serverless inference infrastructure that handles the complexity of production LLM deployment. Qiao raised a $250M Series C in October 2025 led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, Index Ventures, and Evantic, reaching a $4B valuation. Her technical credibility and focus on inference optimization have positioned Fireworks as a go-to platform for enterprises deploying LLMs in production environments where latency and cost matter. 7. Hugging Face: Clément Delangue, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: New York, NY | Total Funding: ~$395M | Valuation: $4.5B Clément Delangue co-founded Hugging Face and turned it into the central hub of the open-source AI ecosystem. The platform hosts pre-trained models, datasets, and AI applications, providing model hosting, fine-tuning, and inference APIs that have made Hugging Face essential infrastructure for over 100,000 developers and enterprises building with AI. Delangue has built one of the most capital-efficient companies in AI, achieving a $4.5B valuation while maintaining deep community trust, a combination that is rare in infrastructure. Hugging Face’s position as the “GitHub of AI” gives it a strategic role in the enterprise AI stack that extends far beyond any single product: it’s where models are discovered, shared, and deployed, making Delangue one of the most quietly influential CEOs in the entire AI infrastructure landscape. 8. Labelbox: Manu Sharma, Founder & CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: ~$189M Manu Sharma founded Labelbox to solve the data labeling bottleneck that constrains every ML team. The platform provides tools for creating high-quality training data at scale, combining workforce management, quality assurance, and collaboration tools for labeling complex data types including images, video, text, and audio, the unglamorous but essential work that determines whether ML models actually perform in production. Sharma has built Labelbox into a platform trusted by major enterprises for data preparation, serving 50+ significant customers with 449 employees as of early 2026. While data labeling may lack the headline appeal of model training or inference, it remains one of the most persistent bottlenecks in enterprise AI, and Sharma has positioned Labelbox as the infrastructure layer that ensures enterprises can feed their models with the high-quality data they need. 9. Lambda: Stephen Balaban, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: $1.5B+ Stephen Balaban co-founded Lambda as a GPU cloud provider and has scaled it into what the company calls a “superintelligence cloud,” providing bare metal GPU instances, optimized NVIDIA Blackwell clusters, and dedicated supercomputing capacity for large-scale AI training and inference. Lambda differentiates from general-purpose cloud providers by focusing exclusively on AI workloads and offering infrastructure optimized specifically for that use case. Balaban secured a multi-billion dollar partnership with Microsoft for tens of thousands of GB300 NVL72 GPUs and is building a Kansas City AI factory planned for 2026 with 24–100+ MW capacity. Lambda was also a launch partner for NVIDIA’s Vera CPU and quantum networking at GTC 2026. Balaban’s focus on purpose-built AI infrastructure, rather than trying to be a general-purpose cloud, has carved out a significant position in an increasingly competitive GPU cloud market. 10. LangChain: Harrison Chase, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: ~$260M | Valuation: $1.25B Harrison Chase co-founded LangChain and built it into the most widely adopted framework for building AI agent applications with large language models. The platform provides tools for composing LLM chains, managing memory, implementing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and orchestrating multi-step AI workflows, the developer infrastructure that sits between foundation models and production applications. Chase raised $125M in October 2025 at a $1.25B valuation and expanded the platform with LangSmith for agent engineering and observability, plus partnerships with NVIDIA on AI agents. In a landscape where everyone is building AI agents, Chase has positioned LangChain as the picks-and-shovels infrastructure layer, a bet that the framework for building and deploying agents will be as valuable as the agents themselves. 11. Modal: Erik Bernhardsson, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: New York, NY | Total Funding: ~$111M | Valuation: $1.1B Erik Bernhardsson co-founded Modal to make serverless GPU compute as simple as writing a Python function. The platform lets developers run data processing, ML inference, and computational workloads at scale without managing infrastructure, abstracting away the complexity of GPU provisioning, scheduling, and scaling behind a clean API that data scientists and ML engineers actually want to use. Bernhardsson, who previously built the ML infrastructure at Spotify, achieved unicorn status in October 2025 with an $87M Series B and is reportedly in talks for a Series C at a $2.5B valuation as of early 2026. Modal’s developer-first approach has resonated with thousands of ML teams, and Bernhardsson’s bet that simplicity will win in AI infrastructure, even as the underlying compute grows more complex, has produced one of the fastest growth trajectories in the space. 12. Monte Carlo Data: Barr Moses, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: ~$236M | Valuation: $1B+ Barr Moses co-founded Monte Carlo to create a category that didn’t previously exist: data observability. The platform monitors data quality, lineage, and anomalies across data pipelines in real time, catching data issues before they corrupt ML training sets, break dashboards, or produce incorrect model predictions. It’s the data equivalent of application monitoring, and it’s become essential as enterprises realize that AI is only as good as the data flowing through it. Moses raised a $135M Series D that valued Monte Carlo at over $1B, making it the first data observability unicorn. Her thesis, that enterprises need to monitor their data with the same rigor they monitor their applications, has proven prescient as AI deployments proliferate and data quality becomes a board-level concern. Fortune 500 companies now rely on Monte Carlo to ensure the data feeding their AI systems is trustworthy. 13. Pinecone: Ash Ashutosh, CEO Headquarters: New York, NY | Total Funding: ~$138M | Valuation: $750M Ash Ashutosh was appointed CEO of Pinecone in September 2025, replacing founder Edo Liberty to lead the next phase of growth for the managed vector database that has become foundational to the RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) architecture powering most enterprise AI applications. Pinecone provides serverless vector search infrastructure for connecting enterprise data with generative AI models, enabling the “grounding” that makes LLM outputs relevant and accurate. Ashutosh brings enterprise scaling experience to a company that rode the generative AI wave to ubiquity: thousands of enterprises now use Pinecone for vector embeddings and semantic search, and the technology has become essential infrastructure for any organization deploying RAG-based AI applications. His mandate is to convert that adoption into enterprise revenue and expand Pinecone’s role in the AI stack beyond search into broader data infrastructure. 14. Prefect: Jeremiah Lowin, Founder & CEO Headquarters: Washington, DC | Total Funding: ~$46M Jeremiah Lowin founded Prefect to build modern workflow orchestration for data and ML pipelines, the plumbing that ensures data processing, model training, and inference pipelines run reliably, on schedule, and at scale. The platform manages over 200 million data tasks monthly through Prefect Cloud, providing the automation and observability that data teams need to keep their ML infrastructure operational. Lowin has built a capital-efficient company trusted by Fortune 50 organizations including Progressive Insurance and Cash App, with a team of 137 employees delivering disproportionate impact. In an AI infrastructure landscape dominated by GPU clouds and model serving, Lowin has carved out a critical niche in the less glamorous but operationally essential layer of workflow orchestration, the infrastructure that keeps everything else running. 15. Qdrant: André Zayarni, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: Berlin, Germany | Total Funding: ~$87.5M André Zayarni co-founded Qdrant as an open-source vector search engine and has built it into one of the leading vector databases for enterprise AI applications. The platform provides optimized vector similarity search for semantic search, recommendation systems, and RAG implementations, the core retrieval layer that makes generative AI applications contextually aware and enterprise-relevant. Qdrant raised a $50M Series B in March 2026 for “composable vector search infrastructure” and has built a massive open-source community: 29,000+ GitHub stars and 250+ million downloads. Zayarni’s open-source-first approach, familiar from the playbooks of MongoDB, Elastic, and Redis, gives Qdrant a developer adoption base that proprietary competitors struggle to match, and his Berlin headquarters makes Qdrant one of the most prominent European companies in the AI infrastructure space. 16. RunPod: Zhen Lu, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: Remote (US-based) | Total Funding: ~$22M Zhen Lu co-founded RunPod as a globally distributed GPU cloud offering on-demand GPU instances and serverless inference capabilities at a fraction of the cost of major cloud providers, up to 90% savings by the company’s estimates. RunPod’s pay-as-you-go model has made GPU compute accessible to a long tail of developers and small teams that can’t afford reserved capacity from the hyperscalers. What makes RunPod remarkable is its efficiency: with just $22M in funding, Lu has built the platform to over $120M in ARR (as of January 2026) and 500,000 developers. That capital efficiency, driven by Lu’s focus on operational leverage and global GPU sourcing, has made RunPod one of the most compelling unit economics stories in AI infrastructure, and a company that punches far above its weight relative to better-funded competitors. 17. Scale AI: Jason Droege, Interim CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Valuation: ~$29B (post-Meta investment) Jason Droege became Interim CEO of Scale AI in June 2025 after founder Alexandr Wang joined Meta. Droege inherited one of the most important companies in the AI data infrastructure stack: Scale provides the data labeling and AI training infrastructure that enterprises and AI labs use to create high-quality labeled datasets for model training, handling complex annotation tasks across images, text, audio, and video at massive scale. Scale’s valuation reached $29B after Meta acquired a 49% stake valued at $14.3B+, a deal that validated Scale’s position as critical infrastructure for the largest AI training runs in the world. Droege’s challenge is navigating Scale’s evolution from a data labeling company into a broader AI infrastructure platform while managing the company’s complex ownership structure. Wang, who became the youngest self-made billionaire at 24, remains a significant shareholder and board director. 18. Snowflake: Sridhar Ramaswamy, CEO Headquarters: Bozeman, MT | NYSE: SNOW | Market Cap: ~$51.6B (April 2026) Sridhar Ramaswamy became CEO of Snowflake in February 2024 and has been aggressively positioning the data cloud giant as an AI infrastructure company. Snowflake’s platform, which houses massive volumes of enterprise data, is increasingly the foundation layer for AI workloads, providing the data warehouse, data sharing, and compute infrastructure that enterprise AI teams build on top of. Ramaswamy, a former Google SVP who ran the $100B+ ad business and previously co-founded AI search startup Neeva (acquired by Snowflake), brings both AI credibility and enterprise scale experience. Under his leadership, Snowflake has launched Cortex AI (for building AI applications on Snowflake data), Arctic (open-source LLMs), and Document AI, moves designed to ensure that the massive volumes of enterprise data already in Snowflake become the training ground for enterprise AI. 19. Together AI: Vipul Ved Prakash, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: San Francisco, CA | Total Funding: ~$534M | Valuation: $3.3B Vipul Ved Prakash co-founded Together AI to build an AI acceleration cloud optimized for open-source and enterprise AI workloads. The platform provides GPU clusters, distributed training infrastructure, and inference capabilities, with 200 MW of secured power capacity and plans to deploy 36,000+ NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 GPUs with Hypertec, positioning Together as a dedicated infrastructure layer for organizations that want to train and serve their own models rather than relying solely on API providers. Prakash raised a $305M Series B in February 2025 at a $3.3B valuation, making Together one of the best-funded AI infrastructure startups in the world. His thesis, that the future of enterprise AI includes significant on-premise and private cloud model training, not just API consumption, has resonated with enterprises that need control over their AI infrastructure for performance, cost, or compliance reasons. 20. Weaviate: Bob van Luijt, Co-Founder & CEO Headquarters: Amsterdam, Netherlands | Total Funding: ~$68M Bob van Luijt co-founded Weaviate as an open-source vector database and has built it into one of the three leading vector search platforms alongside Pinecone and Qdrant. Weaviate provides a cloud-native vector database with built-in vectorization modules, hybrid search (combining vector and keyword search), and multi-modal capabilities, designed specifically for the RAG and semantic search use cases that power enterprise generative AI applications. Van Luijt’s open-source approach has built strong developer adoption and community trust, and the company’s Amsterdam base makes it, alongside Qdrant in Berlin, part of a growing European presence in AI infrastructure. As vector search becomes a standard component of the enterprise AI stack, van Luijt’s focus on developer experience, multi-modal support, and cloud-native deployment has positioned Weaviate as infrastructure that enterprises are increasingly building into their production AI architectures. Weaviate’s GitHub repository reflects its open-source roots. Who Did We Miss? The AI infrastructure landscape is evolving faster than perhaps any other category in enterprise technology. The global AI data labeling market size accounted for USD 2.30 billion in 2025 and is predicted to increase from USD 2.83 billion in 2026 to approximately USD 18.23 billion by 2035, expanding at a CAGR of 23.00% from 2026 to 2035. The market is driven by the growing adoption of AI, the rising need for high-quality labeled datasets, and the evolution of automated and AI-assisted labeling solutions. Key Takeaways North America led the AI data labeling market in 2025.

Asia-Pacific is expected to grow at the highest CAGR during the forecast period.

By sourcing type, the outsourced segment led the market in 2025.

By sourcing type, the in-house segment is expected to grow at the highest CAGR during the forecast period.

By data type, the text segment dominated the market in 2025.

By data type, the image segment is expected to grow at the highest CAGR between 2026 and 2035.

By labeling method type, the manual segment led the market in 2025.

By end user type, the automobile and mobility segment led the market in 2025.

By end user type, the healthcare and life sciences segment is expected to expand at the highest CAGR from 2026 to 2035. What is the AI Data Labeling Market? The AI data labelling market is the industry that offers tools, platforms, and services to annotate raw data such as images, videos, text, and audio so that it can be used for training machine learning models. This is a crucial step in supervised learning, where machine learning models use labeled data to make predictions. The market has been expanding rapidly due to the growing use of AI in areas such as autonomous vehicles, healthcare, finance, and retail. As AI models become more sophisticated, there has been a growing need for high-quality and large-scale labeled data. Technology Shifts in the AI Data Labeling Market The market for AI data labeling is undergoing a transition from manual, human-intensive labeling to more automated and intelligent approaches. There is a growing adoption of AI-assisted labeling solutions, where the AI model pre-labels the data, and human efforts are primarily used for validation and correction of the data. There is also a significant drift towards the use of synthetic data, which assists in the development of training data without solely depending on real-world data. Another significant transition is the inclusion of human feedback mechanisms, especially in training large language models, where humans rank and then define the results rather than merely labeling the data. The labeling task is also expanding to multimodal data such as video, audio, and 3D sensor inputs, especially in the context of autonomous vehicles and immersive technologies. There is also a growing adoption of continuous data pipelines rather than static datasets, which assist in real-time model updates. What are the AI Data Labeling Market Trends? Collaborations and Partnerships : Companies are establishing partnerships for handling large-scale and complex data labeling tasks. These partnerships leverage AI technologies, cloud infrastructure, and human expertise to enhance accuracy and efficiency. For instance, Appen collaborated with Google Cloud to provide high-quality labeled datasets that are seamlessly integrated with cloud-based AI solutions.

They are also expanding globally while incorporating AI-powered quality assurance systems.
